page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The following contains the text found within The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy, 2021 edition, relating to the first Mass Effect game. Unless otherwise stated, the text was written by Casey Hudson, Derek Watts, Chris Hepler, Karin Weekes and Ryan Cormier.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: **The Mass Effect Team at BioWare**: *The Art of the Mass Effect Universe* was originally published in 2012, covering all the games of the *Mass Effect* trilogy. Since then, the series has continued through multiple expansions; a fourth game, *Mass Effect: Andromeda*; and a completely remastered edition of the trilogy, *Mass Effect Legendary Edition*. We celebrate the art and craftsmanship that went into those three original games with this new edition of the book\-\-*The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy: Expanded Edition*. With additional material from downloadable expansions, multiplayer missions, and extended endings, we hope you'll enjoy the most complete collection of *Mass Effect* trilogy artwork ever published. Thanks for continuing to share this journey with us.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: **Casey Hudson, Executive Producer**: *Mass Effect 3* represents the achievement of an incredible goal: a major video game series that was envisioned as a trilogy from the very start. More importantly, it is a trilogy where *players* decide how the story unfolds\-\-the consequences of their decisions impact not just one game, but the entire series. The two biggest challenges in accomplishing this ambitious plan were that each game had to become popular enough to warrant a sequel, and\-\-even harder\-\-that each game had to get finished; both things are rarities in a winner\-take\-all industry where games are often delayed or canceled altogether. Not only did our team at BioWare drive each game to completion, but each installment went on to became a commercial and critical hit. This is a testament to the talent and professionalism of the artists at BioWare, and to their creative vision for the *Mass Effect* universe. In the eight years that we worked on this trilogy, we watched the *Mass Effect* universe take shape, from the first tentative brush strokes in 2004 to the spectacular realism of the worlds experienced in *Mass Effect 3*. While we always intended to give players an expansive new universe to play in, we never could have imagined the response we've had from fans around the world. For them, and for us, *Mass Effect* is more than a video game\-\-it has become a place filled with the memories of friendships, rivalries, wondrous visions, and thrilling adventures. It has been an honor and a pleasure to work with the art team in the creation of the *Mass Effect* universe. This book is a record of that artistic journey, and I hope you enjoy it. **Derek Watts, Art Director**: When Casey and I sat down and started talking about *Mass Effect*, the project's code name was SFX, and the rest was open territory\-\-a scary thought when presented with the task of visualizing a new universe that needed to resonate with the audience, stand out from the crowd, and be rich enough to carry the license long after the completion of the original game. When conceptualizing the *Mass Effect* universe, we kept a few artists and architects in mind. We drew inspiration from Syd Mead, John Harris, John Berkey, and Santiago Calatrava\-\-just a few of the visual mavericks we looked to. We pored over thousands of images and countless movies to draw every bit of reference we could obtain. It has been fascinating to see *Mass Effect* grow over the years. In the beginning, we were constantly compared to other games and artists, and then, as the series grew and matured, we started hearing how other games were looking like ours. People are looking at products coming out now and are saying, "Hey, that looks like *Mass Effect*!" It is impossible to do justice to the monumental task it was to build a project of this scale. The passion and dedication of the hundreds of artists, drawing over ten thousand concepts and working countless hours, doesn't fit between two covers. Without them, the vision for the universe would have failed, and *Mass Effect* would've been just another title on a long list of forgotten games. I hope this book serves as a window into our artists' minds and shows how they helped create the universe called *Mass Effect*.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: |  | ***“This mission just got a lot more complicated.”*** — Spoilers for **Mass Effect** follow. |  | | --- | --- | --- |

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Matriarch Benezia's appearance is designed to capture the beauty and mystical power of the asari, while bearing the dark and mysterious qualities that helped associate her with Saren. Special attention was given to her headdress, which references religious and royal clothing. Below are early concepts for the asari commando. While a good deal of the concepts had flowing clothing, it ultimately made more sense, from a design perspective, to keep the style military and tight.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: At the top left is an early concept for Saren, depicting him as an older, physically weaker character who still possesses incredibly powerful biotics. The concepts on the right are brainstormed images exploring different aspects of Saren's head, experimenting with structure, scarring, and decorations. We ultimately decided that, unlike most turians, Saren would not have tattoos. We went with a distinctive crest and visible Reaper machinery to reflect his indoctrination. These designs explored different directions for Saren's armor. We eventually decided to show signs of severe indoctrination and Reaper cybernetics by giving him a mechanical arm. We tried several concepts for Saren's head. His final appearance was kept similar to other turians, allowing him to blend into society rather be an obvious monstrosity.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: These quick character studies for the human marines\-\-Ashley, Kaidan, Anderson, and Joker\-\-helped us establish an iconic feel for each character. We drafted many options for armor. Originally, Shepard's armor was red and white, but that made Shepard look too much like a medic rather a combat\-ready marine. Eventually we made the armor charcoal gray and added a red\-and\-white stripe, as well the iconic N7 logo. Although Shepard's armor changed with each subsequent game, these elements remained consistent. Clothing concepts for the people of 2183 included designs for miners, prisoners, prostitutes, and even colonists wearing HAZMAT suits. Through standardizing these concepts, we found a common visual language for human characters.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: To add a familiar element of science\-fiction fantasy, we decided one of the main species in *Mass Effect* would be a race of beautiful blue alien girls. An extensive exploration of the idea led to the asari appearing exotic and alien while still having some human qualities, which allowed them to be desirable as potential love interests. The original inspiration of the scalp tentacles was to evoke the image of a woman emerging from the water with her hair swept back. Asari clothing was to be alluring and sexy but with a sense of class and style\-\-more of a Hollywood red\-carpet feel than that of a stripper (except for the asari who were, in fact, strippers). Once we established the general look of the asari, we examined the fine details, like the scalp tentacles.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: As Linus Pauling once said, "The best way to have a good idea is to have a lot of ideas." We had a lot of ideas for alien species! The writing department came up with an idea for a bird\-like race, and we ran with it... in many directions. From this, the turians emerged with avians legs and an eagle\-like head with the crest of a plumed bird. They have several decidedly unavian feature to keep them alien, like the carapace that shields them from the radiation on their home planet. At the top are designs of turian bodies, including the final form. Most of the aliens in *Mass Effect* were designed without clothing or armor. Adding them later in the process forced us to keep designs consistent and complete to avoid having models with missing aspects hidden under clothing. Below are variations of turian heads. Once we had the head design, we tried to work out decorations to give each individual turian a unique look. The top concepts are various styles of turian armor, including light and heavy versions. For their clothing, we balanced the design between human and alien, allowing space for turian head crests, the bones jutting from their calves, and the carapace on their shoulder blades.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The krogan were designed to be a race perpetually at war. They are obviously semireptilian, but one of their early inspirations was bats. The reference for the krogan body was the heavy skin of an Indian rhinoceros. To make Wrex stand out from the crowd, we gave him a splash of color on his head crest and deep scars across his face. This made it clear that he'd seen major combat. The concepts above show facial expressions that helped animation. Below that are models used to figure out coloration, including the final model of Wrex. Early body designs for the krogan (*facing page*) included large ape\-like creatures. A lot of these needed to be scrapped because of animation limitations. Above is a variety of krogan armor, including multiple helmet designs and versions for heavily armored bosses. Below that are variations of krogan clothing. Since krogan are almost never seen out of their armor, these were rarely used.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The salarians were our version of "gray aliens," but with a nearly concave torso and dog\-like legs. These unique body features set the guidelines for all the clothing and armor to follow. The bottom collection represents the steps it took to reach final drawings of the salarian head as well as examples of how one of the variations might show emotion. We do drawings of expressions to help us figure out how the aliens will emote using digital acting system. A wide variety of concept sketches of clothing for salarians. Except for a few of the drawings, most of them were too human to meet our needs.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Tali'Zorah presented a challenge. We needed to create one alien who would, for a time, be the only example of her species. All we knew about the quarians was that they were a scavenger race that created the geth. When some of these drawings were done, we didn't yet know what the geth actually looked like. Eventually, we decided on a look for the geth that influenced the lower quarians drawings. Tali was to have her face covered by a mask, tantalizing the player, who could barely make out the shape of her eyes, but no more. Here you can see the influence the geth had on Tali's design, ranging from the very geth\-like on the far upper left to the final designs on the lower right. The breathing mask and clothing became the envirosuit. The quarians, having a weak immune system, won't live long outside an envirosuit.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: In the early conception phase, anything and everything is possible. Some of the more outrageous original designs for the elcor are featured below. Eventually, modeling and animation constraints influenced the design.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The volus are another race of of aliens that need a full\-body envirosuit. Volus are from a planet with high air pressure, and to remove them from their suit anywhere else would cause them to rupture, much like a deep\-sea fish brought to the surface. Some concepts for their species were relatively large. Ultimately, they became short and round, giving them a docile look.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The geth are the most common enemy in the game, so they needed to stand out from enemies in other science\-fiction universes. The head design was first nailed down for the geth armature, and this later became the basis for the geth's head design. The production painting at the top shows how the geth hopper might attach itself to the wall, like Spider\-Man clinging to a building. The middle images show variations refining the geth, such as the body playing and the shape of the head. The bottom images are variations on the final look of the geth hopper.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The Thorian was lovingly referred to as the "grotesque sac" around the office. It developed into a fungal creature that was thousands of years old and able to infect humans with mind\-affecting spores and to create clone duplicates of a creature it had absorbed.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Early concepts for the rachni queen imagined what she would look like captured in a containment tank. We pictured her never being fully illuminated\-\-a mysterious figure. Inspiration came from deep\-sea creatures. Eventually, the queen's design came closer to that of a rachni soldier or worker to clearly indicate they were the same species. We gave her a larger abdomen, since it was important to the story that she was capable of birthing a vast number of rachni. We toyed with a wide variety of ideas for the rachni. The original thought was to design a creature with long arms that could reach out and pierce the player. Eventually, these arms became something closer to whips.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The Citadel represents the seat of galactic government and thus was the level most representative of *Mass Effect*'s architectural style. With large swooping curves cutting across vertical lines, it aimed to define *Mass Effect*'s look. The actual design was inspired by a sculpture that had five sides and a ring. The five sides became the ward arms, each one a city the size of Manhattan. The ring became the Presidium. Later, we attached the Citadel Tower, where the council members sit. We designed a 3D model to help visualize the Citadel's ability to transform from an open station into an impenetrable shell. The top images on the opposite page show early visualizations of the Citadel's interiors. The bottom image on the opposite page is the Presidium's interior\-\-the utopia of tomorrow\-\-a perfect blend of nature and architecture. We referenced NASA concepts, including the Stanford torus design. Early Citadel concepts also had windows looking out into space, which were eventually discarded when the design confused testers.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Originally, Virmire was to be a tropical paradise, a vacation spot for galactic travelers. The inspiration for the rock formation was the Phi Phi Islands in Thailand. The buildings were connected by floating walkways and attached by structures built into the rocks\-\-nature and architecture working in harmony. This all changed radically. Virmire became Saren's base of operations, making the paradise theme unusable. The design shifted to "nautical fortress," complete with massive concrete walls and heavy gun batteries. Some of the original concepts remain in the level, such as the floating walkways and the open\-air environment.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Therum was originally a base built around the opening of a volcano. The base was going to be built up around the caldera, with heavy equipment mining the molten rock. Instead, the level was redesigned as an underground dig site.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: What's a science\-fiction game without an ice planet? Noveria originally had a lower alpine section, with the research stations high among the peaks. Eventually, we removed the lower section because it made players think they were on two different planets. The mountaintop station, Peak 15, was designed to look camouflaged. It was so massive that it blended right in with the other peaks. The top drawings are concepts of Peak 15's interior. The idea behind these was that encased tubes (affectionately called "hamster tubes") would be suspended within the ice and rock.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The original idea for Eden Prime, inspired by England's Lake District National Park, had blue skies and rolling green hills. The Eden Prime colony farmed this area and created large towers with a suspended rail system for transporting crops. Later, we decided that Reapers had destroyed Eden Prime by the time Shepard arrived. The new design included battle damage and the "scorched sky" seen in the final game.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Ilos originally felt like El Dorado or other legendary cities lost deep within a jungle, but having several tropical planets in the game, we decided to change the appearance of the level and to give it a more alien feel. We referenced Zdzislaw Beksinski when reimagining this world. The dried coral replaced the roots and vegetation covering the structures. We also relit the level to give it the feel that everything there was dying, just as the Protheans had.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Feros featured Shepard fighting through war\-torn skyscrapers linked by bridges. We wanted to push the epic nature of kilometers\-tall superskyscrapers that had been wrecked by the geth. When the player arrives, only a few remain. The images to the left show the hub where the colonists erected shields and barriers to protect themselves, powered by one of their cargo ships.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Early concepts for the *Normandy* explored the ship as a fighter, a cruiser, a smuggler's ship, and a stealth vessel. Eventually it became a military prototype with a large crew and sufficient cargo space to store the Mako. Despite the fact that it lands on planets, we purposely never put visible landing gear on the *Normandy*\-\-it hovers. When it docks on stations like the Citadel, arms extend and attach to the ship. *Normandy*'s final design referenced delta\-wing fighters and the Concorde, giving it an aggressive, futuristic look. The concepts below and to the right were made to visualize the wide variety of machinery on the *Normandy* and throughout the *Mass Effect* universe. These images are concepts of the *Normandy*'s navigational and loading\-bay areas. We needed to create a space where a large crew could live comfortably for months at a time.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Our goal to create an expansive universe meant drafting concepts for the galaxy's many different ships and vehicles. The Alliance ships referenced the design style of the *Normandy*, with large bidirectional thrusters. At the bottom are concepts that eventually became a krogan truck and an asari\-designed skycar.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: We had many concepts for the Mako. We tried it as a rover, a tank, and a scout vehicle. In some concepts it even hovered, an idea that resurfaced with the Hammerhead in *Mass Effect 2*. Eventually, we decided to reference a modern armored personnel carrier. We gave it a darkened armored\-glass front and six wheels, which became the standard for *Mass Effect*'s heavy vehicles.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: We had more concepts for helmets, of all things, than anything else in the *Mass Effect* universe. We made over two hundred types in trying to figure out what Shepard's helmet should look like. We went back and forth between a closed\-face helmet, for a more futuristic feel, and an open\-faced helmet, similar to those in use by militaries today. We decided to go with the open\-faced helmet so that players could see characters' expressions during the game's conversations.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: We were cognizant of the fact that giving ships faster\-than\-light travel wasn't necessarily enough to account for a galaxy\-spanning civilization. To address this, we came up with mass relays, which used superior alien technology. The early designs varied widely, but we eventually settled on an unused concept for the Citadel, fitting since the Citadel and the mass relays had a common designer.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: There is an expansive array of corporate logos, military insignias, and other symbols in the *Mass Effect* universe. Some images below were adopted for the Citadel or the Alliance. Others were stamped on the ubiquitous crates as logos for shipping companies.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: *Mass Effect*'s guns had to be collapsible so that the player could store several on Shepard's back. The concepts on top were the weapons the player would have at the beginning of the game, and all have the strong *Mass Effect* arch. The original guns were chrome, later changed to make them more practical for military use. The guns were all designed with two barrels, mainly for appearance rather than functionality. The four holes on the original assault rifle were for slotting in modifications. This was later altered in favor of color variations, but the slots remained in the weapon's design.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The geth ships looked like metallic insects. The bottom images were concepts for the geth cruiser, dropship, and fighter, showing how it might be animated while flying. Small arms were attached to the geth vehicles to give them the look of a fly rubbing its legs together. Since the geth were the most common enemy in the game, we tried a wide variety of weapons and machinery for them. One original concept was a cyborg with dolphin\-like skin, as seen on the facing page at top left, but we felt this would be difficult to present convincingly. The idea was scrapped in favor of a metal appearance.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: Some concepts for machinery were used on the main worlds as set dressing, while others were made for the uncharted worlds where Shepard retrieves technology lost on the surface of the planet. Given the size of the *Mass Effect* universe, we needed an enormous amount of set dressing and ambient machinery like chairs, beds, storage, and medical equipment to make the areas look lived in and believable. They aren't the most glamorous pieces, but if they didn't exist, players would feel something was missing.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: The double pair of eyes that gives batarians their unique appearance was the most challenging part of their design. This aggressive race was the first four\-eyed alien created at BioWare, and it was new territory in facial construction.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect
text: *Bring Down the Sky* was the first *Mass Effect* DLC ever released. It introduced travel to the Asgard System and included what some players deemed a "fiendish" choice between killing a batarian named Balak and saving a group of human hostages he's holding. Shepard is tasked with disengaging three large fusion thrusters that are pushing the X57 asteroid into the orbit of a neighboring planet\-\-and a probable deadly collision. page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy
text: **The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy: Expanded Edition** is a 264\-page concept art book published by Dark Horse Comics LLC in 2021 containing BioWare artworks and developer commentary for the games Mass Effect, Mass Effect 2 and Mass Effect 3. Originally released in 2012 under the name **The Art of the Mass Effect Universe**, the 2021 edition contains over 90 additional pages of artwork focused on the trilogy's downloadable content and Mass Effect 3's multiplayer. Developer commentary found in both editions was written by Casey Hudson, Derek Watts and Chris Hepler, while the Expanded Edition's extra commentary was also contributed by Karin Weekes and Ryan Cormier.

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy
text: The *Mass Effect* games are an epic of groundbreaking immersion, introducing the richest science\-fiction universe of our generation. Now BioWare and Dark Horse are proud to invite fans deeper than ever into the *Mass Effect* saga! Featuring never\-before\-seen concept art and commentary by BioWare on the games' characters, locations, vehicles, weapons, and more\-\-including *Mass Effect 3*\-\-*The Art of the Mass Effect Universe* is the most complete companion available to gaming's most compelling series!

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy
text: Expanded with never\-before\-seen artwork, this new edition delves deeper than ever into the sci\-fi saga that changed video games forever. Contains extensive new material from the DLCs for all three games\-\-including the award\-winning *Lair of the Shadow Broker* from *Mass Effect 2* and the fan\-favorite *Citadel* from *Mass Effect 3*. Experience the evolution of the aliens, planets, ships, and technology that define this iconic science\-fiction universe. The developers who brought BioWare's masterpiece to life take you from the earliest design sketches to the meticulous final renders. Brimming with concept art and commentary, this expanded edition is the ultimate companion to one of the greatest series in the history of gaming!

page: The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy
text: After a brief preface signed by "The Mass Effect Team at BioWare" found only in the Expanded Edition, the book opens with separate introductions by Casey Hudson and Derek Watts. The rest of the work is divided into the three games, containing felt sketches, design concepts, production paintings, 3D renders and accompanying commentary for the trilogy's visual elements. Developer commentary can be found on most pages, which was written by the following people, who have all worked on the trilogy except for Cormier: - Casey Hudson: game director - Derek Watts: art director - Chris Hepler: writer - Karin Weekes (Expanded Edition only): editor - Ryan Cormier (Expanded Edition only): editor A copy of each game's commentary can be found here: - The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect - The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect 2 - The Art of the Mass Effect Trilogy/Mass Effect 3 ## - Ebook: ISBN 978\-1\-50672\-164\-4 - Hardcover: ISBN 978\-1\-50672\-163\-7 - BioWare Gear Edition: ISBN 978\-1\-50672\-576\-5

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 1: The Beginning of the End
text: The following is a transcription of the first chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 1: The Beginning of the End
text: When Casey Hudson looks to the frigid sky above his backyard in Edmonton, Alberta, he doesn't see blackness. He sees possibility. "The vastness of what could be up there is just so awesome," he suggests to me one night in January 2012, invoking his favorite adjective to conjure up thoughts of other galaxies or civilizations. As he looks up into the minus 35 degree air, the distant light signatures of Venus and Jupiter flicker behind his white puffs of breath. Unshaven, with his curly black hair tucked inside an Edmonton Oilers baseball cap, he's come outside after 15 hours of work not to look up, but to take care of what's below: a patch of ice that he waters every night as a makeshift skating rink for his two young boys. The steam from the warm water evaporates into the air, and Hudson has a fleeting moment of calm. He knows there isn't much time for stargazing. Not tonight. The event horizon that is the final hours of game development is an all\-consuming black hole, and Hudson's new game, Mass Effect 3, will soon be finished. Now it's just a question of how painful the last few days will be. But until it's done, tomorrow, Saturday, will be just another day at the office. If you arrive in Edmonton and ask some folks where to find BioWare, they wouldn't be wrong if they told you, "Look for the nondescript office building with the dermatologist, pub, and hotel with a big GET FIT IN 2012! light\-up sign." Saturday morning around 9 a.m., Hudson pulls his Audi TT — with 130,000 miles on the odometer — into the front parking lot of this strange complex with no visible sign for BioWare, one of the world's most respected video game developers. The back of his car is covered in mud, completely camouflaging the Alberta license plate. The car wash can wait. Mass Effect 3 can't. Here, on the third floor, Hudson and a mighty team of Canadian programmers, artists, designers and writers are crafting one of 2012's most ambitious and anticipated video games. Set about 175 years in the future, Mass Effect has transcended its medium with books, comics, action figures, iPad games, clothing and even a forthcoming movie from Legendary Pictures. Ihe overarching science fiction world is memorable, but Mass Effect's real innovation comes in the way its story adapts to choices made by individual players. Like a cutting\-edge choose\-your\-own\-adventure book, a supporting character can live or die, or a world can prosper or perish, all based on the profound story you make as hero Commander Shepard. (To further increase the immersion, you can pick whether Shepard is male or female.) The ways to play through Mass Effect are as vast as the possibilities that exist in the night sky above Edmonton. The matrix of choices is nearly infinite, but the team is focused on something more definite: the final 175 bugs or "open issues" that must be fixed. Long gone are the days of dreaming up fanciful new characters, vast worlds and emotionally piercing dialogue. As he walks through the Byzantine blue\-walled corridors on the Mass Effect floor, designer Preston Watamaniuk sums it up best: "A game is a bit like an oil tanker. The closer you are to the end of the journey the less room you have to maneuver," he says. With so many possibilities, the testing phase of Mass Effect 3 requires scientific precision. Monitors in the hall use real\-time charts and graphs to track how many issues remain, not unlike the way TV networks update voting results on election night. At any time the chart can change and a department will be put on notice to plug up the leak in the oil tanker. Watamaniuk reinforces that point with an email he sends out to the entire group: "The policy this weekend is simple," he writes. "Everyone is on call. If you get a bug that has been triaged by the leads you must fix it immediately." "Triaged" is a term used to describe a process in which Hudson, Watamaniuk, lead programmer David Falkner and the other core team members sit around a conference room and go through every single outstanding issue. Munching on peanut butter cookies, they sit for hours and debate bugs. Today's most pressing hitch: On the PlayStation 3 a game will crash if the player leaves it sitting on the multiplayer main menu for six straight hours. Hudson sits at the keyboard and "sends back" the problem for someone to fix. Every day the number of bugs decreases — they hope — until the team hits zero. That's when Mass Effect 3 is officially sent to certification.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 1: The Beginning of the End
text: "Triaged" is a term used to describe a process in which Hudson, Watamaniuk, lead programmer David Falkner and the other core team members sit around a conference room and go through every single outstanding issue. Munching on peanut butter cookies, they sit for hours and debate bugs. Today's most pressing hitch: On the PlayStation 3 a game will crash if the player leaves it sitting on the multiplayer main menu for six straight hours. Hudson sits at the keyboard and "sends back" the problem for someone to fix. Every day the number of bugs decreases — they hope — until the team hits zero. That's when Mass Effect 3 is officially sent to certification. Walking out of the conference room after Saturday's triage, Hudson sneaks over to the microwave to heat up his Starbucks quad Americano. You can tell he's worn down but completely focused on not disappointing BioWare's faithful fans. A quote from Mass Effect 3 perfectly sums up his state of mind. "The end of the world reminds you what you forgot to do," Admiral Anderson says as the Reaper aliens invade Earth. In this case it's the trilogy that's ending, and Casey' Hudson doesn't want to be the guy who forgot to wrap up a plot line that fans want to see resolved. As he walks back to his desk and opens up his email, Hudson knows he is just hours away from saying goodbye to a series that has consumed nearly a quarter of his life. Now, as the final arc of Commander Shepard's story arrives, it is time to tell the tale of how this group of eclectic Canadians — including a garbage man, a furniture truck driver and a local theater actress — came together to create a franchise that has pushed the narrative potential of gaming in bold new directions. Along the way there have been moments of triumph, challenges to overcome and dark hours of creative despair. These are the final hours of Mass Effect 3\.

section: Video: Casey Describes His Typical Workday
text: **Casey Hudson**: So, my typical day would be... I get up, and I make breakfast for my boys. Even when when we were doing ninety\-hour weeks, I made sure that, every morning, I made breakfast for my boys, drove my son to school, and then in the evening, I'd be there for bedtime, even if I had to come home for bedtime, and then go back. Usually, my day, in a typical day will be, you know, sort of a combination of meetings. Usually, it's meetings to go over the story, or we'll sit down and look at a system that we're trying to design and, you know, I'll, you know, help make decisions about what we should be doing and try and provide some direction there, whether it's technical or creative. If it's kind of early production, maybe I'm home in time for supper and then I can spend time with my family. And otherwise, I'll come home and put the kids to sleep and then come back. And that's what we were doing in the last phase where, you know, we were just cycling through hundreds and hundreds of bugs and tasks per day; and I would just come back to work and then work until, you know, eleven or twelve o'clock at night.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 12: The Letter on the Door
text: The following is a transcription of the twelfth chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 12: The Letter on the Door
text: What would the first day of the rest of Casey Hudson's life feel like? Today, February 13, is that day. Mass Effect 3 is finished and while there is more work to do on downloadable content, the detachment process has begun. Casey had thought about this day over the years and was never sure what it was going to feel like. Although he doesn't want to admit it, he kind of wishes he was still working on the game. But for now, with no triage meeting on the books and his Outlook calendar strangely bare, he decides to finally take me to see his airplane at a hanger \[sic] about 20 minutes from the office. As we drive along the snowy highways of Edmonton, Hudson begins to reminisce not about the game, but about how beautiful it is to far away from the rest of the entertainment world. He remembers the days when he and his wife — who started dating back in the seventh grade — would go to her grandparent's farm and just run around with no sense of place or time. He wants the same for his kids, and that's why he recently invested in a quarter of land — 160 acres outside of Edmonton. Nothing is on the land and that's precisely the point. "You look around and there is just space in every direction. It's like your own little world," he says as we drive down a highway with no end in sight. At one point during the car trip I remember a letter I saw Hudson tape to his office door a few weeks ago. Lots of fan letters come from around the world to BioWare, but for some reason this neatly printed letter resonated with Hudson during the final hours. It came from a young boy named Zachary Sentz, a seventh\-grader from East Berlin, Pa. "I am just wondering if maybe you and some of your co\-workers could figure something out to make the trilogy a little longer," the young boy asked. More than just asking the question, Zachary had some ideas. What if, he suggested, Shepard and his or her true love had a child, and, in a twist similar to *Red Dead Redemption*, you ended up playing as that child. As the child you could "wander and find a cave with a prophecy written on the wall and the child knows what he or she needs to do," he continued, ending the letter with the line, "This is all I've come up with for the idea." There was something poignant and simple about Sentz' letter. And while he never knew it when he wrote it, his letter probably reminds Hudson of the young boy in the post\-credits sequence of the game who asks a man, played by astronaut Buzz Aldrin, if there are other tales of "The Shepard" to be told. This beautiful scene, set at night on a snowy farm in some unknown place, was an important coda for Hudson. Having recently finished the game myself, I asked him about that scene and wondered if it ties into the letter. "Everyone is going to have a different ending to some degree based on their choices and their galactic readiness," he says, "so it was important for me to have one final scene where everyone has the exact same experience." Does the young boy's letter hint at something more, namely that the series continues? While there will definitely be more Mass Effect games and other stories told in the future, Commander Shepard's story has concluded. Hudson isn't sure where the series goes next, but he's pretty confident that he never wants to tell any stories that take place in a post\-Shepard era. "Whatever we do would likely happen before or during the events of Mass Effect 3, not after," he suggests. As we arrive at the hanger, Hudson unlocks the door and inside. Besides his plane he is storing some friends' cars for the winter and a buddy's helicopter across the three bays. He walks up to his plane and begins to flick switches like a video game controller, making sure to show me the cool GPS system and screens that let him see the topography through the clouds as he flies over Jasper. Sensing his fascination with the plane, technology and outer space, I ask him if perhaps his next adventure will be trying to fly into space on Virgin Galactic. To my surprise he says that no, that doesn't really interest him at all. "I'd rather pilot something, not be a passenger," he says as he walks around and inspects his plane. "I want to be in control of where I'm going, what I'm there to do and the choices that I'm making."

section: Video: Casey Discusses the Message of ME3
text: **Casey Hudson**: I think one of the really neat things about video games, as a medium, is that there can be a message in them, without making a statement. You know, with with a passive medium like a book or a movie, you know, it kinda has to... it can raise questions, and I think that's usually what people respond to the best is, when a movie raises a question that makes you think about it. Sometimes, it makes a statement. But the great thing about a video game is that you can explore an issue, and let a player explore their thoughts on the issue interactively. And so, you don't have to say something specifically about, for example in Mass Effect 3, the idea of organic life and synthetic life, and... whether synthetic life will ever rival our intelligence, and whether we should incorporate technology more and more into our bodies, and things like this. You can explore those ideas, and experience some of the consequences and think about, you know, what you think is right, without the game having to make a statement on it. And to me, that's more interesting. Chapter Navigation | ← Previous Chapter |  |  | | --- | --- | --- | | The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 11: The Perfect Illusion |  |  |

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 4: Codename SFX
text: The following is a transcription of the fourth chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 4: Codename SFX
text: It was September 2003, almost a decade ago, when Casey Hudson sat down for lunch with Ray Muzyka and Greg Zeschuk at Yiannis Taverna on Whyte Avenue in Edmonton. Hudson was finally ready to share some of the ideas that had been stirring in his head about the team's next science fiction game. The working title the team came up with was SFX, and Hudson had great ambitions, as outlined in a one\-page document he presented to the doctors. The first line said it all: "With online capabilities and gameplay features that will redefine the genre, SFX will become a mainstream phenomenon and a must\-have game for the Xbox 2." Hudson's vision was to create a game somewhere between the turned\-based role playing of KOTOR and the fast\-paced action of the sci\-fi shooter Halo. He imagined a rich story with memorable characters, exploration in a spaceship like his favorite game Starflight, and a robust online feature in which fans could trade and share the spoils of war over Xbox Live. There were no details yet about the main character or the story, but Hudson did have one thing figured out: He wanted the doctors to commit to making a trilogy of games in this unknown and unnamed universe. Yes, he wanted BioWare to make its own Star Wars. So taken aback by Hudson's bold ambition, Muzyka burned his tongue on some hot soup at lunch and still remembers it to this day. Although initially shocked at the bet\-the\-company scale of Hudson's proposal, the doctors couldn't fault him. The truth was, they'd long evangelized the idea of BioWare creating its own worlds, not borrowing others like D\&D and Star Wars. Microsoft, eager to publish a BioWare game after the success of KOTOR, expressed early interest in making the trilogy exclusive to the new Xbox. Hudson was given the green light to begin exploring ideas with his core team from KOTOR. A launch date was projected for about three and a half years down the road, in 2007\. That may sound like a long time, but the team knew they couldn't rush the development of the game's overarching fiction. In fact, plans called for the core SFX team to spend the entire first year working on the universe with little regard for game development. Every day the team would sit around a conference room table for four hours and debate the most basic questions about their sci\-fi. How far in the future will it be set? Will there be aliens? What about time travel? Karpyshyn remembers the discussions playing out like a real\-time message board thread where the team debated the merits of every recent sci\-fi property including Star Trek and Babylon 5. In one meeting Joss Whedon's *Firefly* was discussed. Hudson hadn't seen it, so he was given the DVDs to watch as homework. (He ended up liking it more than he thought he would.) Eventually, the team zeroed in on the idea of a universe set in the near future, but with a twist that would allow for faster\-than\-light travel: the discovery of ancient alien technology. The hero would be modeled after a Jack Bauer or James Bond—like character who could act with impunity in outer space, doing whatever is necessary to keep intergalactic peace. As discussions continued, Derek Watts began sketching ideas for the world and characters might look like. When he threw down a concept piece of a dinosaur with a gun, the team instantly fell in love and thus the Krogan \[sic] were born. Budget concerns made everyone realize they wouldn't be able to create male and female versions of all the aliens, so plans were drawn up to include an all\-female alien race, the Asari. \[sic] Watts also began conceptualizing ideas for Star City, a Manhattan\-like hub for the player's operations that would later be known as the Citadel. In January 2004 Hudson and the team wrote a document titled "Master Slaves" that helped crystallize the overarching plot. The concept was that a now\-extinct alien race, then known as the Nazari, had left behind technology that unlocked the possibility of faster\-than\-light travel, interconnecting the galaxy like never before. Eventually, humans would discover this technology and the fact that they were a slave race created by the aliens to do their bidding, hence the name "master slaves." What the team still hadn't figured out was how this discovery would take place or how it could be turned into a three\-act story. Would the aliens somehow return to the present day? And if not, who would be the adversary? Karpyshyn took a stab at answering some of these questions in his first pass at the story.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 4: Codename SFX
text: The concept was that a now\-extinct alien race, then known as the Nazari, had left behind technology that unlocked the possibility of faster\-than\-light travel, interconnecting the galaxy like never before. Eventually, humans would discover this technology and the fact that they were a slave race created by the aliens to do their bidding, hence the name "master slaves." What the team still hadn't figured out was how this discovery would take place or how it could be turned into a three\-act story. Would the aliens somehow return to the present day? And if not, who would be the adversary? Karpyshyn took a stab at answering some of these questions in his first pass at the story. Originally the game starred a human hero named Captain Anderson (yes, you read that right) who would face off against Saren, a villain with a mosquito's stinger coming out of the back of his head. Saren would lead a warmongering race of small bat\-like creatures called the Batarians who were hell\-bent on stealing the alien technology. That head\-to\-head conflict between Anderson and Saren was a good start, but if the story of SFX was to span three games, the team needed a theme more universal than a race to find an alien artifact. That theme would soon emerge from an unlikely place: a Japanese research lab. Developed by Japanese researcher Hideyuki Sawada, the KTR voice robot was an unnerving experiment. Sawada's goal was to see if a robot with soft silicone lips could imitate the sounds of the human mouth using artificial cords. Watamaniuk found a video of it on YouTube and started playing it in the team meetings. At first its repetitious annunciations were absurd and funny, but eventually the team began to think about its implications. Was Raymond Kurzweil right? Within 30 years could we really reach that point of singularity where man and machine are indistinguishable? If that crucible is forthcoming, the tension between organic and synthetic life could be an appropriate theme to frame the SFX trilogy. "When you think about it, any civilization out there that's more advanced than us is probably peaceful," says Hudson. "Everyone has to go through the crucible of developing nuclear weapons and either destroying themselves or passing through that." At a high level, Mass Effect could be the story of the next crucible a civilization faces, when technology rivals organic life. A rise of the machines plot is nothing new in the annals of science fiction, but the team came up with a unique twist to build on the master slaves idea. Perhaps the machines had risen to power long ago, and now, ominously lurking in deep space, decide to return and harvest sentient life as fodder for a machine army. To strengthen the machine versus human overtones, they excised the bat army in favor of a robot army named the Geth. \[sic] At first Watts and his team imagined the Geth as organic beings with synthetic fluid running through their veins, similar to Bishop from Aliens. Eventually, however, the Geth evolved into the current robot\-like form. After a year and half of deselopment the game still was carrying the codename SFX. The team debated a series of names such as Space Age, Element Zero, Threshold and the Epsilon Effect, but could never come to an agreement. One day Hudson walked into the room and said, "What would you guys think of naming the game Rainbow?" Everyone was momentarily shocked until Hudson finished his thought: "Rainbow....Six, the Tom Clancy games." The point was that the name didn't really matter. Eventually co\-founder Zeschuk surfaced the name Mass Effect, which tied into the idea of the science behind the game's "mass relay" time travel devices, and the concept of one individual being able to change the course of history. Two years into development Mass Effect was starting to take shape as a science fiction property. The actual game, however, was in a far worse state. In order to up the action, BioWare had licensed Epic Games' Unreal Engine, the same technology behind the Gears of War series (and Infinity Blade on iPad). Focusing on action was an uncharted territory for the team, and there were growing pains as they tried to balance tactical combat with fast\-paced action. Levels had been designed on planets such as the snowy world of Noveria, but there was little in the way of focus. Hudson would play the level and then call in Watamaniuk to ask, "What exactly is supposed to be happening on this level?" No one knew the answer. The levels were being built in a vacuum, with little knowledge of how they'd eventually fit into the story.

Frustrated, Hudson came into the office one Saturday during the summer of 2005 and realized that the game wasn't making the progress he wanted to see. The plot wasn't fully fleshed out, the gameplay was unfocused, and no one was happy with the design of the main character, now known as Commander Shepard, who looked a bit like a medic, not the Jack Bauer of space. After years of experimentation, the pressure was starting to mount. Microsoft was planning to announce the game at a press event in October 2005\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 4: Codename SFX
text: - Casey's first pitch document for what became Mass Effect. Tap for a closer look. **SFX (September 15, 2003\)** --- - A spectacular new Sci\-Fi roleplaying game and IP created by BioWare. With online capabilities and gameplay features that will redefine the genre, SFX will become a mainstream phenomenon and a must\-have game for the Xbox2\. **Imagine** - SFX takes place in a thrilling futuristic setting, with a combination of familiar locations and exotic worlds. - It is the dawn of the interstellar age, with only a few explored worlds and many more accessible via exploration. - Sleek vehicles and vistas create a uniquely identifiable look to the universe, while rendering techniques depict the player's experience with a stylish ultra\-realism. **Play** - An epic BioWare story will be at the center of the powerful, character driven story. - Gameplay will build on the elements from SW:KotOR \- but will be more accessible to the mainstream audience. - Players will lead a small party of 2 or 3, selected from a larger group of adventurers. Players can switch to control other party members at any time, and characters not controlled by the player will perform player\-designated actions and AI scripts. - The combat system will allow dazzling combat choreography and intense ranged combat, but will also be more responsive than a round\-based system. - Players will be able to freely explore a galaxy of procedurally generated planets in an upgradeable starship, to obtain valuable items and resources. Players can explore areas freely, or travel to special locations as part of the single\-player story. - Xbox2 Live support will allow an additional dimension of gameplay through trading and communicating with players around the world. - Story progression, planetary exploration, and online trading will create an emergent style of gameplay that is unprecedented in the RPG genre. - Because of the Xbox 2 Live capability and the procedural galaxy exploration system, the game continues limitlessly beyond the end of the single\-player story. **Trade** - Through Xbox2 Live, you can meet friends online in special locations in the game to chat and trade valuable items in a virtual environment. - Some items found in the game will be different from one Xbox2 system to another, and they can be combined with other items online to create powerful new items not available without online trading. - A dynamic in\-game economy will make trading online compelling, as precious items may be valued differently from one Xbox2 system to another. - Xbox2 Live can also tie the entire SFX community together in other exciting ways, such as the addition of new locations, special items, new quests, and online news updates about the best players. **The SFX Project \- Development Strengths** - SFX will be developed by the team that developed SW:Kotor. Their experience will be directly applied to making a bigger and better RPG franchise on the Xbox2\. - SFX will be developed on a new engine, custom tailored to push the Xbox2 to its limits through a focus on realistic lighting, physics, and render quality. **Target Release: 2007** - Gallery: How the Quarian Race Has Evolved - Left: early concept work on Saren, a potential villain. Above: the first\-ever in\-game character created for SFX. - The Master Slaves plot for SFX is revealed for the first time. Tap for a closer look. **Master Slaves (January 8, 2004\)** --- 1. **Hook**: Humanity has recently drawn the attention of the many powerful alien species competing for control of the galaxy, all of whom have based their cultures on the not fully understood technology left behind by a now extinct creator race. Though scientifically inferior, humanity has suddenly become an important species in the galactic community because of our inherent ability to use this ancient technology. **Extra details:** Travel across great distances is accomplished through the use of jump stations/hyper gates left behind by the creator race. Upon discovering and activating one of these gates on Mars, humanity has opened up our system to the galactic community as a whole. Within the galaxy there are numerous powerful alien empires struggling against each other to expand their spheres of influence. These aliens have established a galactic council on Star City, a gigantic space station that serves as the political and economic hub of the galaxy. Each of these species sees humanity and their affinity for the creator technology as both a potential threat and a potential resource that can be exploited for their own advancement. 2. **Basic Criteria**: a. **Concept Twist**: Humans were engineered as the slave class of the creator race millennia ago. b. **Special Character**: You an \[sic] elite human that has become an important tool to both the Earth and the aliens.

The player will visit established worlds of the various alien empires, as well as exploring uncharted or undeveloped areas to establish new jump stations and expand the galactic frontier. d. **Moral Compass**: The character could work for some military/civilian agency that is trying to establish humanity in the greater galactic community. The Star City is a central nexus for explorers like the character hunting down important artifacts and information. Instead of constantly returning to Earth an embassy could be established so that the character has easy access to aliens and agency \[sic] they serve. 3. **Start Location**: Earth 4. **Time Period**: Near Future 5. **Setting**: Familiar technology but enhanced via the alien technology on earth. \[sic] Alien technology can be more advanced and unfamiliar. 6. **Space Travel**: The character travels locally by using faster than light drive. However for long distance trips Jump Gates are used. These gates are a good way of opening up new zones of exploration for the player. You can travel between stars locally out to X light years but if you want to travel a greater distance a gate must be used. In this way we could open up new star clusters to explore and better control the flow of the game. Each cluster could also have an over arching theme, story\-line or purpose. 7. **Aliens**: a. Quantity: Aliens are common once the player leaves Earth b. Species: Many different species. c. Interaction: Interact similar to modern nation states. d. text: The following is a transcription of the sixth chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 6: That Which Is True
text: Caroline Livingstone couldn't afford to buy her son the Nike shoes he wanted. That got to her. As a working actor in the Canadian public theater scene, Livingstone traveled with her young son from city to city around Western Canada. One week the single mother was playing the Wicked Witch of the West in a production of the  *Wizard of Oz* in Regina, Saskatchewan; the next, a role in *Spring Awakening* in Edmonton. Caroline loved the way being on stage made her feel, and if she was being honest, that was just about the only good thing about being a local theater actress. "It's a tough, poor life," she recalls. Then one day her friend Shauna called with a proposition. Would Caroline be interested in performing the voice of the healer in Neverwinter Nights, a new game from BioWare? She said yes, one thing led to another, and before long Livingstone stepped into the role as BioWare's in\-house producer and director of voice\-overs. Her arrival couldn't have been more perfectly timed. Hudson and the Mass Effect team had grand visions of building a game with emotional resonance, but that was possible only if the players believed the voice\-over performances. The "digital acting" in Mass Effect, like most games, was still quite primitive. But somehow the combination of well\-directed line reads with subtle effects like blinking, expressive eyes and natural, motion\-captured movements gave organic life to these virtual characters. When Mass Effect arrived in November 2007 the digital acting and the strongly developed characters were cited in most reviews as the game's strong point. And while the game was generally well reviewed, there were complaints about the vehicle, the Mako, being hard to control, annoyances with the combat system, and extremely long level load times that were presented as elevator rides to new locations. By Christmas 2007 Hudson was happy the game was out the door and selling well, but couldn't help but feel a little disappointed. "It didn't initially hit with the impact that I probably hoped that it would," he now admits. Still, there were signs that something special was starting to happen. Right around Christmas a letter arrived at BioWare. The writer's son, who suffered from Asperger's syndrome, had difficulty with nonverbal communication skills. But after playing Mass Effect and learning how to judge emotions in a safe environment, the boy started to be more outgoing in real life. The line between reality and games was starting to blur. That introduced a host of new complications. One of the team's early goals with Mass Effect was to create a believable in\-game romance between two characters, assuming the player chose that storyline. Hudson imagined these romances as a three\-act love story that could play out over the entire trilogy. In the first game male protagonists could mate with Ashley; females with a male soldier named Kaiden; \[sic] and both characters could unlock a "paramour" with Liara, an Asari \[sic] female alien. Those options were good enough for most players, but same\-sex relationships were not possible. "We'd get letters from fans who would say, 'You're offering all the choices except the ones I want,'" remembers Hudson. No one wanted to frustrate the fans, but the outcry underscored the perils of player choice. How do you balance what players want to do with the notion of defined characters? How far should a game let you take your choices before the traits of the character "Commander Shepard" disappear and he or she becomes nothing more than a mindless vessel acting out the users' whims? The exclusion of same\-sex romances was a hot button issue, but the same struggle between player agency and defined storytelling applied to many other facets of the game, such as the decision by the developers to kill off a character for story reasons when certain players don't want it to happen inside of "their" world. The debate over the romances in Mass Effect extended as far as Fox News when, in a January 2008 report, Cooper Lawrence, a misinformed, gun\-for\-hire social pundit, blasted the game for its supposedly graphic "alien sex scenes" that were corrupting the minds of young boys. Lawrence, whom, as I pointed out on the air, had never played the game, much less developed a romance in it, was later forced to publicly recant her comments in *The New York Times*. It was early 2008 in Jasper, Alberta. After more than four years of hard work on Mass Effect, the team members were beginning to think about a sequel and trying to throw their lives back into balance. One weekend Hudson invited Watts and lead artist Mike Trottier to hike up Pyramid Peak in Jasper, a mountain Hudson sometimes still climbed with his father.

text: Lawrence, whom, as I pointed out on the air, had never played the game, much less developed a romance in it, was later forced to publicly recant her comments in *The New York Times*. It was early 2008 in Jasper, Alberta. After more than four years of hard work on Mass Effect, the team members were beginning to think about a sequel and trying to throw their lives back into balance. One weekend Hudson invited Watts and lead artist Mike Trottier to hike up Pyramid Peak in Jasper, a mountain Hudson sometimes still climbed with his father. After finishing some beers and hot dogs, the trio started hiking and began to reflect on how much their had changed during Mass Effect. Each now had children and joked that they already knew what was in store for the next half decade: two more Mass Effect games and raising their kids. Realizing how structured his life had become, Hudson decided he wanted to challenge himself to do something new. Well, something new as in something he hadn't done in a long time. Sixteen years after he last piloted a plane, he suddenly had a desire to fly again. In the spring he put a four\-seat Diamond Star XLS prop plane on order and started the process of renewing his pilot's license. Before the plane arrived he told friends that he might even get it painted the colors of the *Normandy*, the player's spaceship in Mass Effect. Back at the office, Hudson spent time thinking about Mass Effect 2. He put together a huge spreadsheet that analyzed all the positive and negative feedback about the game from 97 different reviews. And in a black notebook labeled "SFX," he began charting out ideas for the sequel. If Mass Effect was the wake\-up call about the pending Reaper invasion and the third game was to become an all\-out war against them, he, Karpyshyn and Mac Walters needed a good second act to the story. (Karpyshyn left the team shortly after Mass Effect 2 began production to focus on the development of BioWare's latest release, the massively multiplayer game Star Wars: The Old Republic.) Walters and Hudson centered in on a dirty dozen story in Shepard would spend the second act of the game canvassing the galaxy to recruit what he called "commandos" in his notes. This diverse group of characters — including familiar faces from the first game — would team up with Shepard to fight a mysterious force known as the Collectors. Somehow tied to the Reapers, these aliens were wiping out human colonies around the galaxy. The second game would culminate in a battle, a so\-called suicide mission in which many of the characters could — including the player's Commander Shepard. The sequel also gave Walters a chance to bring back his idea for the shadowy organization of Cerberus, only briefly hinted at in the original game. Hudson ran with this idea and suggested that the organization be run by a character he imagined would look like Anderson Cooper from CNN and act like Jack Bauer's brother Graem from 24, a rogue charlatan who had enough power to tell the president of the United States what to do. The character would be known as the Illusive Man, a self\-appointed protector of humanity who would do whatever is necessary — even outside the political system — to ensure the race survives and controls the Reapers. Martin Sheen was selected as the voice of the character. Other changes were on the table for the sequel. For a while, the team wanted Shepard's ship, the *Normandy*, to be destroyed at the start of the game as part of his untimely demise. (The Illusive Man would bring Shepard back to life and help him assemble a new ship, named the Leviathan, in the first act of the story.) Watts and the art team pushed back because they loved the Normandy design and the interiors, inspired by the George Clooney movie Solaris. Eventually the design team relented; the ship was blown up at the beginning, but it was replaced by the nearly identical *Normandy SR\-2*. One element of the game that definitely needed refinement was the combat. Although the team had envisioned Mass Effect as being as easy to play as Halo, the mechanics in the first game weren't nearly as refined. Cover was difficult to use, players had to pause the game to activate special powers, and the health and ammunition systems weren't as seamless as other games. Corey Gaspur, a young designer who has his arms covered in black tattoos inspired by comic book artist Bernie Wrightson, co\-wrote a memo to Watamaniuk to suggest significant overhauls to the sequel's gameplay.

text: Eventually the design team relented; the ship was blown up at the beginning, but it was replaced by the nearly identical *Normandy SR\-2*. One element of the game that definitely needed refinement was the combat. Although the team had envisioned Mass Effect as being as easy to play as Halo, the mechanics in the first game weren't nearly as refined. Cover was difficult to use, players had to pause the game to activate special powers, and the health and ammunition systems weren't as seamless as other games. Corey Gaspur, a young designer who has his arms covered in black tattoos inspired by comic book artist Bernie Wrightson, co\-wrote a memo to Watamaniuk to suggest significant overhauls to the sequel's gameplay. Space combat was briefly considered as an addition but was dismissed early on so the team could focus on refining the core action mechanics. BioWare wanted to keep its core role\-playing fans happy but at the same time it wanted to compete with shooters like Gears of War. Still, the debate about whether Mass Effect was a "shooter" or an "RPG" would rage on online message boards. Had BioWare abandoned its core fans to build an action game like Halo or Gears of War? "The whole debate is rather silly," offers Watamaniuk. "Battlefield 3 is a shooter with great progression and upgrades, does that make it an RPG? Both of these game genres are blending together." First announced in early 2009, Mass Effect 2, all things considered, had a relatively smooth development process. Still, the scope of the game was monstrous, featuring up to 12 different potential squadmates and a massive endgame battle against the Collectors, who were trying to construct a new Reaper out of harvested human remains. With so many new characters in the mix, Hudson and the writers made a conscious decision to largely exclude Ashley and Kaiden, \[sic] the main love interests from the first game. "That was all by design," Hudson explains to me one evening in his office as he looks at a photo of his wife in Times Square. "I wanted Mass Effect to be a three\-act love story, and missing your love throughout the second game was exactly how I wanted players to feel." When it arrived in early January 2010, Mass Effect 2 received the highest scores Electronic Arts had ever seen for one of its games. (BioWare was acquired by Electronic Arts about a month before Mass Effect arrived in November 2007\.) All the great ideas from the first game — the branching plot, the memorable characters and the richly realized universe — had been made even better, and most of the key issues from game one had been addressed. Even though it arrived in late January, critics started saying Mass Effect 2 was a contender for game of the year. *Time Magazine* raved that Mass Effect was the "Avatar of videogames—except it's better written." Fox News decided to sit this one out. Mass Effect 2 finally became the phenomenon that Hudson had hoped for the first time around. Now came the even tougher part: trying to wrap up the trilogy with an even better sequel.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 6: That Which Is True
section: Video: Hudson on Player Reaction to Characters
text: **Casey Hudson**: We knew from the beginning of the Mass Effect series that this was going to be a big focus for us\-\- is technology around creating characters that could act with emotion, and then trying to use that technology in ways we've never done before, where maybe a character can just look at you and you feel an emotion from... just on that look. And so, we developed those kinds of things, and it was intentional that that would be kind of a new thing for this series, but we actually had no idea how much of a reaction that we would get from players, to these characters. We've always had romances in BioWare games going back to Baldur's Gate, but we've never really had this kind of reaction to characters in a game, where people, you know... it's almost like these are real experiences and real relationships that people want to see more of, and they demand time with certain characters in each game that we make. And so, we try and build that feedback in. And that's why some of the characters in Mass Effect 2 that had previously not been love interests, like, Garrus and Tali, in their story lines, we worked in love interests. Because, even though we couldn't conceive of it in Mass Effect 1, people saw these characters, like a character like Garrus, very interesting alien character; it wasn't meant to be a lot of interest in the beginning, but because he acts with emotion and real humanity, people want to get to know him better.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 8: Devastatingly Impactful Choices
text: The following is a transcription of the eighth chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 8: Devastatingly Impactful Choices
text: When he isn't at home painting Warhammer 40k figures or spending time with his twin 5\-year\-old daughters, Preston Watamaniuk is thinking about Mass Effect. As Hudson's right\-hand man on all three games, he can complete the original Mass Effect in a one\-hour\-and\-38\-minute speed run. (This, incidentally, is 3 minutes shy of the world record.) If anyone on the team has a question about a possible way to play through the game, they usually ask Watamaniuk, because he has completed each one about 60 or 70 times. Besides bragging rights, Watamaniuk's hardcore play style yields a real benefit during team meetings. Since he knows all the ways to play the game, he also knows what different groups of fans are expecting. Asked to give an example, he points to a scene that was added during the final two weeks on Mass Effect 2. In one of his final play\-throughs Watamaniuk realized that the team hadn't created a payoff for players who remained faithful to their romantic interest from the first game. This, it should be pointed out, was not an easy thing to do. Ashley, Kaiden \[sic] and Liara were hardly seen in Mass Effect 2 on purpose, and temptations were introduced throughout the story. There was no time to record dialogue for a new pay\-off scene, but Watamaniuk was adamant that the game needed to acknowledge a player's loyalty to his or her digital squeeze. The compromise was a simple yet poignant scene in which Shepard longingly looks at a photo of his love interest in his quarters. "It's the little moments like that which make our games different," says Watamaniuk. "Even if that moment only happens for a couple thousand people out of millions, it's worth it." There was also the issue of what to do for the millions of people who fiddled around on the side during Mass Effect 2\. (You're busted: According to statistics revealed for the first time in this story, more than 70 percent of players fall into this camp.) Watamaniuk told the team that he wanted a "massive consequence" for these cheaters when they inevitably run into the romantic interest from the first game during the events of Mass Effect 3. The consequence of cheating led to a deeper discussion about the aftermath of choices in the third game. Mass Effect 1 and 2 had decision points that changed elements of the plot and switched around characters, but it wasn't as if all those choices always had sweeping consequences. Killing Wrex, for instance, would change some dialogue and cause him to be replaced by another Krogan, \[sic] Wreav, in Mass Effect 2\. Characters could die at the end of Mass Effect 2, but their fate was usually sealed by choices made earlier in the game by the player — not a heat\-of\-the\-moment dialogue decision. For the third game the team wanted players to agonize over decisions with devastating consequences on both sides. "If we did it right players will hopefully say, 'Man, I'm really not sure if I made the right choice,'" says Walters. Two main plot mints were identified as having the biggest opportunity for impact. The first was the resolution of the ongoing war between the Quarians \[sic] and the Geth, \[sic] the robot AIs that became sentient and revolted against their masters. The second was tied to the genophage, a long\-running theme in the series. A new cure would be manufactured by the Salarians \[sic] and it would be up to the player to decide whether it is deployed. It's one of the game's finest moments, as you agonize over the decision and have multiple opportunities to change your mind. There is no right or wrong path, but the decision has a dramatic impact on the galaxy and the player's experience during the rest of the game. In practice most players will make one choice, and then, after completing the game, head to YouTube to discover what could have happened if they pushed the story in another direction. One other choice the team made during Mass Effect 3's production was to introduce same\-sex relationships for both male and female players. The topic was a subject of much debate both online and inside of BioWare. Ultimately the writers and designers had to balance the player's right to free will with the fact that you are playing the role of a defined character that may have its own sexual preference. Hudson and the team opted to open up the possibilities, but only after first making sure the voice actors were comfortable with the decision. "Hopefully the way we depict love in the future is the way it will be in the future," he says. The ways players could experience Mass Effect was expanding, but the production schedule was not.

section: Video: Mac on the Genophage Decision
text: **Mac Walters**: I really wanted to sort of set up this betrayal with Mordin, or Padok Wiks, earlier on, so that you actually had opportunities as you were going along to say "hey, these guys are trying to screw you over." But then, also the opportunity to say nothing. And I'm glad we\-\- and it's something we haven't done before, and nobody was quite sure that that was gonna work, and how that would feel, but it's funny; it's one of those things where people have come back since and go like "that was awesome. It's like I kinda wanted to tell him, but then I didn't." Sylvia, I think it was, or the writer working on that, had this amazing idea of why don't we use an Interrupt where, you know, Mordin or Padok are actually walking away from you slowly and you have this opportunity to shoot them in the back. And it was kind of a unique way of using the interrupts that we haven't used before, because... it's not just\-\- it's not the obvious "I gotta kill this person" Interrupt; it's the "what the hell do I do here?" And we actually slow down time and you have to think about it and it's just like... in the end, I think, you know, the debates we had over how to pull that off are great because people have played it. They're just like, "oh my god. I can't believe, you know, I was forced to make that decision. I don't even know if I made the right decision." So... You know, sort of, I think fighting over that sort of how to bring a personal sort of side to that epic decision, was one that took a long time to come to fruition. But in the end, I think we did a great job with it.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3
text: **The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3** is a documentary work published by journalist Geoff Keighley in March, 2012, around the time of the release of Mass Effect 3. Through exclusive anecdotes and interviews with BioWare, it covers the origins of the studio and the inception of the first Mass Effect game all the way to the end of development for Mass Effect 3\. The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3 was originally released in an interactive document format allowing for link embeds, as well as music and videos, which became deprecated in the following years. In consequence, the "original" version was removed from sale, though a truncated Kindle version remains available. Following the release of Mass Effect Legendary Edition, Electronic Arts uploaded the original version on their website as a freely downloadable bonus requiring Adobe Air to open, though a number of functionalities remain broken.

**Location:** Milky Way / Artemis Tau / Knossos System /  **Second planet**

**Therum** is a distant but rich industrial world claimed by the human Systems Alliance. Its plentiful heavy metals have fueled the recent manufacturing boom on Earth. Core samples rich with the fossils of simple silicon\-based organisms indicate Therum was more habitable in the past than it is at present. Perhaps this explains the many Prothean ruins dotting the surface, most of which have been looted by mining corporations.
- *Mission:* Find Liara T'Soni

- In the demo footage for Mass Effect, there was a mission on a planet named Caleston that involved rescuing a group of miners who had been trapped underground by the geth attack.
