For the weapon in Mass Effect 2 and Mass Effect 3, see M\-9 Tempest.* | | --- | --- | The **Andromeda Initiative Survey Ship Tempest** is a scout ship used by the Pathfinder team to explore various worlds across the Heleus Cluster in the hope of finding suitable homes for Milky Way colonists in the Andromeda galaxy. Between missions, Tempest is the Pathfinder team's home, and everything in it is state of the art. |  | ***“Make no mistake — this is a one\-way trip.”*** — Spoilers for **Mass Effect: Andromeda** follow. |  | | --- | --- | --- |

The Tempest was originally one of several purpose\-built ships for each ark's Pathfinder team. Kallo Jath was part of the team that designed and tested the Tempest and its prototype. Because the Initiative needed absolutely up\-to\-date technology for its construction, some of it were procured through dubiously legal means. When the Nexus struck the Scourge after arriving in the Heleus Cluster, the other Pathfinder ships were destroyed, making the Tempest one of a kind. Before the arrival of Ark Hyperion, Nexus leadership had planned to dismantle the Tempest for its parts, but Vetra Nyx protected the ship.

The Tempest is divided into three decks, each with rooms whose functions are vital to the success of the Pathfinder's mission. Deck 1 is accessible via twin ramps from Deck 2\. Going from Deck 2 to Deck 3 and vice versa can be accomplished via multiple access ladders or a cargo bay lift.

Practical applications of intel and samples gathered like upgrading weapons, armor, and the ND1 Nomad are done in the research room, supported by discoveries from the ship's tech and bio labs. It is situated at the ship's approximate center on Deck 2, between engineering at the aft and the tech and bio labs at the fore. Additionally, Strike Teams missions can be launched from a terminal in this room. This is the location of the Research Center on the Tempest. The holographic projector table displays a representation of the location pertinent to the Pathfinder's next major course of action.

Technological items are sequestered and studied at the tech lab. It is located on Deck 2, just opposite the bio lab in the fore section of the ship. Jaal Ama Darav establishes his quarters at the tech lab. Research ongoing here include comparative studies between angaran and Initiative tech and possible blended applications.

The bio lab has containment and analysis facilities for biological samples like plants and wildlife. It is located on Deck 2, just opposite the tech lab in the fore section of the ship. Cora Harper takes care of the hydroponics in the lab during her downtime. The number of plants in hydroponics increases as a result of progression through the cluster.
The meeting room, situated toward the upper aft section of the Tempest, is a place to gather the crew or hold video conferences with the Nexus or other parties. It is the only chamber on Deck 1\.
At the aft section of Deck 2 is the engineering room, housing the starship's drive core. Gil Brodie monitors here when he's not around other parts of the ship.

The Pathfinder team's armory, where weapons are stored while off\-mission, is on Deck 3 aft section. According to Kallo, there are secret compartments here. Vetra Nyx has appropriated this place for supply storage and other requisitions.

Another facility on Deck 3, the med bay has beds armed with a variety of medical equipment to diagnose and treat potential injuries. This is also the location where a Respec Station can be found. Dr. Lexi T'Perro can be found here when she's not on other parts of the ship.

The cargo bay on Deck 3 houses the ND1 Nomad scout rover. It opens up the underbelly of the Tempest to deploy the vehicle or the ground team itself on a ramp. Other miscellaneous items in the cargo bay include a Forward Station and an inoperative EVA module regularly tinkered on by crew members.

The crew are housed in two wall\-set two\-man bunks in an area with ample space and greenery on Deck 3, below the bio lab. Adjacent to it is a bathroom with a two\-shower system separate from the single toilet. The Crew Info Board is found here. There's also space for a coffee machine and a desk for computer work on opposite sides.

The galley functions as the ship's kitchen and dining facility. An L\-shaped seater with a table opposite the cooking area plus a couple of swivel chairs forms the room's structural arrangement. The galley supplies start out as meager rations from what little the Nexus has to spare. As the team progresses through the cluster, it eventually becomes stocked with fresh produce from newly\-founded outposts as well as newly\-discovered trading partners. Nakmor Drack claims the galley as his quarters upon joining the crew, though he can be found more often on other parts of the ship.

The Pathfinder's cabin is generally off\-limits to the crew unless invited inside. It is the exclusive abode of the ship's commander. Amenities present include a sitting room, a music system, a wardrobe, display shelves for model ships, a window to (or a projection of) space taking up an entire side, and far larger living quarters compared to the crew's. It is on Deck 3, directly below the bridge. SAM has a terminal next to the model ship displays. An e\-mail terminal next to him can be used to access and acknowledge incoming messages. If a Space Hamster has been acquired, it can also be seen here on a transparent cage with ample food.

This is where the ship's pilot steers the ship and where the Pathfinder operates the navigational system, synced specifically to them. The foremost section of the ship on Deck 2, the bridge also has a wide viewing area displaying the universe ahead. Additionally the Galaxy Map and email terminal can be accessed from this location.

Normally used for the purpose its name suggests, after Peebee joins the crew she adopts it as her own makeshift quarters. Her "pet" Remnant Observer, Poc, is usually kept here after its construction. The room is on Deck 2, beside the bridge.

This is where people disembark in facilities that can accommodate airlock interfaces. Prior to leaving the ship, the Pathfinder can customize their gear in the loadout station here. It is on Deck 2, opposite the escape pods.
The storage room in the Deck 3 aft section has been appropriated by Liam Kosta for his quarters. It has his worn\-out sleeping couch prominent among other items.

Owing to both the Citadel Council's restrictions on civilian vessels bearing military\-grade weaponry, and the Initiative's own emphasis on peaceful exploration, the Tempest completely lacks any external armaments such as torpedo launchers or mass accelerator cannons. Heavy armour and a main gun were traded in the design phase for a vessel that is small, stealthy and fast, capable of both interstellar exploration and subtle infiltration in equal measure. With an IES stealth system derived from the technology first employed by the SSV Normandy, the Tempest can remain hidden from most forms of detection, while its superior speed and maneuverability make it easily able to evade any pursuing vessels should its presence be discovered. The ship's engine is based on the arks' ODSY drive, recycling static energy buildup to power her systems. It took technicians weeks to miniaturize the design for the Tempest, along with several electrical shocks. The Tempest is capable of covering 13 lightyears per day in FTL. Its size allows it to land on planets with little trouble, much like the SSV Normandy and unlike the larger Normandy SR\-2. Four main thrusters provide its propulsion and it has four additional downward thrusters to stabilize its descent: two below the canard and two below the main wings. It is equipped with an array of scanners for determining groundside conditions before landing, along with a dedicated probe bay to help it pinpoint anomalies both in space and on the ground. The "glass" onboard the ship is composed of a clear oxide and nanofiber compound, and will bend rather than break. Stress\-testing the material involved three drunk krogan and a C\-Sec battering ram.

Kallo Jath Test pilot and the only one of the team who departed for Andromeda. Lucille Diawara Lead designer. She broke her back during construction, forcing her to convert a construction mech into a wearable rig. Prior to the Initiative's voyage she glued her rig into the armory (her artist signature) and set it up so that an audio log from her activates once a SAM unit scans the 70\-kilo rig. Lucille seemed to be a fan of William Shakespeare, or more specifically, The Tempest. O'Connell Systems designer. He installed the ship's nav array, which took him a dozen spacewalks to perform. His teammates pranked him one time by messing with his power distribution model when he forgot to lock his terminal: for two days he was convinced turning on all the bathroom lights would overload the engine core. Remembered by Kallo arguing equations with Teon one time. Sorenna Debugger, remembered by Kallo to be stumped on code line 2281\. Worked with Teon for weeks to fit an ODSY drive into the Tempest's smaller profile. She still used her former bondmate's perfume years after they separated. Teon'Adda vas Moreh Quarian aerospace engineer who embroidered intricate patterns on his enviro suit. Resourceful enough to circumvent racism on Omega by using a memory foam glued to his enviro\-suit to make a mold of the drive core components he wanted.

The world is named for an ancient asari goddess of love, sex, travel, and law\-\-spheres of influence whose overlap initially baffled human xenoanthropologists. The journeys necessitated a system of rules governing guests, fugitives, and alliances\-\-all watched over by the goddess Tevura. The Reapers have ignored Tevura so far, its science stations and moon\-based mining equipment offering little strategic importance. page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: The following contains the text found within the fourth part of The Art of Mass Effect, published in 2007\. The commentary was written entirely by Casey Hudson.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Minute details might be the last thing one would think of in the production of an epic videogame, \[sic] but artists must design and build countless small objects to complete the illusion of a functioning world. Some of these objects have an obvious appeal, such as the arsenal of futuristic weapons strapped to Commander Shepard's armor. Others, like beds and computer stations, simply provide context and functionality to each area in the game, while reinforcing Mass Effect's sleek and futuristic art style through their unique designs.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: The primary weapon for geth troopers was designed to have a similar look to their starships, a long curving appearance that resembles an organic exoskeleton. Like all weapons in Mass Effect, the geth rifle folds down to a compact shape for storage.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: The drones were built and controlled by the geth, so they bear similar features\-the \[sic] single blue eye light and vaguely metallic surface.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: This concept shows how the hex barriers were originally meant to be projected from stationary objects. This was later simplified by having the geth create the barriers directly.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: The geth heavy drone (top) provided a fast\-moving enemy, while the flyer (below) was designed to give normal geth troopers a raised platform for attacking the player. Ultimately, Saren would be the only character to use the flyer.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Incorporating shapes from other geth\-made devices, these simple towers provided a high location from which to snipe.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: The geth have evolved into many distinct forms. To create the particularly large and dangerous enemies for Mass Effect, a four\-legged giant was designed. The head\-mounted turret was removed late in development to allow for omni\-directional aiming.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Mass Effect's design sense is particularly prominent in the equipment and appliances that detail the environment. Sweeping arcs meet straight lines to form elegant geometry that seems functional but futuristic.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: While the solar array (below) and drill (above) were primarily decorative, the barrier was heavily used to provide cover during combat.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: The asari Consort makes use of these pods for privacy and comfort, but they were originally meant to hang from the ceilings of the Citadel's seedier establishments to showcase exotic dancers.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Sometimes objects without an obvious purpose are required, so designers can place them in the environment for players to use as interactive objects of tactical cover during combat.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Objects like the escape pod (middle) and the downed satellite (bottom) created opportunities for discovery and exploration on Uncharted Worlds.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Because players are free to explore a wide range of environments in Mass Effect, objects had to be built to detail everything from the exotic to the everyday. Even futuristic versions of desks, chairs, and shelves had to be made to flesh out the homes, offices, and living quarters of various characters.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: One of the most difficult designs turned out to be the human helmets. Because all human armors would share the same basic helmet design and the helmet would frame the characters' faces when they speak in close\-ups, it was extremely important that the design was functional and visually appealing. To ensure that the characters' faces would be seen even while wearing a helmet, a clear visor and a chin guard that did not obscure the mouth were chosen.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Numerous variations on pistol designs were developed to find a balance between futuristic design and present\-day notions of firepower. To create a look that's unique to Mass Effect, all weapons have two barrels, one atop the other.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Since grenades in Mass Effect can fly in straight lines, they were given a compact disc\-like shape.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: In keeping with Mass Effect's heavy use of circular arcs, the upper body of the rifle is defined by a long curve. While some designs ignored this principle they still applied the double\-barrel weapon design (top). The use of arcs is also prominent on the sniper rifle (bottom).

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Though the mechanism would work entirely differently in the year 2183, a short\-range, scatter\-shot weapon was considered to be a valuable weapon for a Spectre's arsenal.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Designers felt that using technology\-based attacks in combat was as important as using conventional weapons. The omni\-tool allows characters to manipulate a holographic interface to instantly release these attacks, in addition to activating such non\-combat capabilities as hacking electronic locks.

page: The Art of Mass Effect/A Galaxy of Details
text: Throwing a starship across the galaxy is no small feat, and Mass Effect's writers and artists had to come up with a believable way to do that. Even after the pseudo\-science was worked out, it was still unclear how they would visually realize it. Some ideas for mass relays were elaborate and mechanical, while others were more monolithic. The final design used heavy rotating rings to create the sensation of building power. Its tuning\-fork shape appeared to focus the tremendous energy into a straight beam that could project a starship many light\-years across the galaxy. The following contains the text found within the second part of The Art of Mass Effect, published in 2007\. The commentary was written entirely by Casey Hudson.

To add life to the worlds of Mass Effect, a galaxy of new creatures and aliens was required. To achieve a truly alien appearance for creatures and monsters, artists combined the features of earthly animals in strange combinations, creating unique new creatures with immediately recognizable traits. In addition to these basic life\-forms, players would meet characters from advanced alien civilizations that would need to interact with the intelligence and emotion of a human being. Developing the anatomy and costuming of these aliens would require an extensive concepting process, as well as considerable reference to earthly cultures and creatures.

To capture a familiar element of science fiction \[sic] "fantasy" fulfillment, one of the main species in Mass Effect was to be a race of beautiful "green alien girls". An extensive exploration of ideas was needed to make them appear exotic and alien while still retaining human qualities allowing them to be desirable as potential love interests. Though they are able to wear clothing and armor meant for human females, special costumes were designed for the asari, ranging from the tight\-fitting armor of the biotic commandos to the alluring clothing of the asari Consorts. In developing an alien species, it is as important to visualize personality and spirit as much as anatomical details. These paintings helped to define the strength and mystery behind the asari.

To create additional species to expand and diversify the populations of Mass Effect, BioWare's artists were free to explore countless ideas for weird and wonderful creatures. From this wealth of creativity, the elcor, volus, and hanar were chosen to become three distinctly different species. The stout and powerful appearance of this concept became a front\-runner for the elcor, but its bipedal stance was considered too human. This painting (right) and its original sketch (above) cemented the design for the elcor. They also provided a definitive (and humorous) perspective on their personality.

In the first story drafts, Saren's geth army was actually a bat\-like species. But as Mass Effect's underlying theme of organics vs. machines emerged, the geth were rewritten as a synthetic lifeform. In contrast to the image of the classic metallic robot, the geth were designed to have a more lithe and sinewy appearance. One image (top left) appropriately captured this disconcerting approach, using rubbery tubing in place of veins and muscle striations. Closing in on the final design, detailed paintings were made to establish material properties and other details that would help the 3\-D artists create the geth, including the single blue "eye" that casts a horizontal lens flare.

The design of human clothing helped establish the sleek and clean future of the Mass Effect universe. Early concepts focused on the graphical shapes and colors that would clearly differentiate characters from one another, such as mechanics, doctors, and bar patrons.

To create a unique and consistent style, all armor designs would be based on the same principles: the use of straight lines and circular arcs to create strong geometric shapes. The final design for standard human armor (opposite, in white) created a futuristic and form\-fitting look while retaining a functional appearance that could be effective in combat. Other armors were required for unique characters, such as the hazmat suit (above and opposite, in red).

To quickly evaluate a wide range of ideas for alien anatomies, small silhouette concepts were produced. Though some of the spider\-like shapes were compelling, they were too similar to some of the other creatures, such as the rachni. Instead, the jellyfish concept (opposite) represented a unique direction for an exotic species. Later concepts developed the hanar into a more slender, lighter\-than\-air creature.

Filling the role of the big, brutish species in the Mass Effect universe, the krogan incorporated reptilian features. The final concept (opposite, top left) brought their design somewhat closer to human proportions, allowing them to move and fight as traditional soldiers.

Creators of the geth, the quarians were overrun by their creations and forced to leave their homeworld. Their visual similarity with geth anatomy helps connect their history. Quarian clothing, seemingly pieced together from scraps, was designed to reflect their nomadic nature. Tali represents the appearance of only one member of her species. What others might look like\-and \[sic] what they might look like under their visors\-remains \[sic] remains a mystery.

To create a very alien and intellectual look, the salarians were inspired by the wide\-eyed, delicate appearance of salamanders. Their bodies and armor were designed to support these qualities by creating a unique profile.

For each species in Mass Effect, a range of clothing styles was required to create characters from various levels of society. The concept for the counselor \[sic] robes (above) was approved as a final design, whereas many early concepts were never build (left).

Knowing that Mass Effect's villain would be a turian, artists gave this species features that would support his intimidating character. The bony face plates give turian characters a stern, hawk\-like appearance, while the wiry body frame implies a potential for stealthy movement.

Sometimes a design seems to have a life of its own. The volus began as a heavily\-clothed character with a gas mask (below) that developed into this lovable and portly final design (opposite). This final drawing inspired artists and writers to transform the volus into a diminuative, comical species.

While the rachni would initially appear as mindless monsters, the rachni queen would be surprisingly intellectual, in addition to being physically intimidating. Though she would be nearly 50 feet long, her design was inspired by tiny beetles and insects.

Early versions of the rachni showed a spider\-like form with deadly pointed arms that could attack with a stabbing motion. These would later become whip\-like appendages that could attack from a greater distance. As the final design of the rachni took shape, ideas for rachni eggs and hive entrances were developed to provide locations for rachni to emerge from.
Although the Thorian was originally written as a plant\-like creature, its design transformed into a more slug\-like appearance, achieving a grotesque and intimidating form.

The harvester was meant to be a very large creature that could only be defeated with the use of the Mako all\-terrain combat vehicle. Althrough its final design (opposite, center) was built, it was never used.

The Mass Effect universe is populated with a number of ambient creatures that give life to the environments. Gas bags (above, right) are lighter\-than\-air creatures that release poisonous fumes when "popped." Man\-sized beetles (above, left) represent no danger but nonetheless, are a remarkable sight.

Creature designs in the Mass Effect universe employ a simple device to make them seem alien: an unnatural combination of familiar earth creatures. The varren are a perfect example of this, combining the body of a dog with the scaly skin and bulbous eyes of a deep\-sea fish.
Possibly the largest creature in the Mass Effect universe, the thresher is able to burst from the soil without warning.
To achieve the appearance of a "gentle insect", the design of the keepers was based on the praying mantis, with whimsical details (a vest and tiny backpack) to make them seem sentient.
In the process of exploring ideas for creatures seen in Mass Effect, many excellent concepts were drawn but not built. A team favorite was the "space goat" (top, right).

|  | ***“Make no mistake — this is a one\-way trip.”*** — Spoilers for **Mass Effect: Andromeda** follow. |  | | --- | --- | --- | **The Cardinal** is the female Ascendant in charge of an exaltation facility on Voeld. She firmly believes in the supremacy of the kett, and sees the work they're doing as a "gift" that must be spread throughout Andromeda.

The Cardinal is first seen inside a temple\-like chamber in the facility giving a "fortunate welcome" to the angara who have been "chosen to be exalted". Following a diversion that Pathfinder Ryder's angaran allies trigger, she is quickly questioned by the Archon if Moshae Sjefa is ready for transport. She replies that she is being prepared for final exaltation, the process of genetically transforming angara into kett. By the time Moshae Sjefa is about to be exalted, Ryder has successfully breached the chamber they're in, prompting the Cardinal to escort the Moshae to a hangar bay. The Pathfinder's team persistently pursues her there, where she challenges them into a fight, all the while frantically shouting to her subordinates to defend the Moshae. After the Cardinal's defeat, she pleads mercy to the Pathfinder, begging to have the base (or temple as she calls it) to be spared. In return, the Cardinal will order to have all captured angara at the base to be released. Jaal Ama Darav votes on keeping the base so that the Resistance can rescue the captives, while Moshae Sjefa declares that the base must be destroyed. If the Pathfinder accepts the Cardinal's offer, she keeps her word and departs the scene. She muses that Ryder's decision is apparently the product of them seeing the merits of becoming a kett. Ryder can disagree by shooting her down, or opt to let it slide. If her offer is rejected, she is dismayed and attempts to stop the intruders, though she's shot dead by Jaal in the process.

Offensive The Cardinal's conventional attack is a targeted electric shock. Alternatively, she can unleash a ball\-lightning\-like attack which conducts electricity to nearby enemies. This heavily\-damaging attack ignores cover and can stagger characters out of it. At close range, she can grab a target in a gravity\-sphere, then collapse the sphere to crush the victim for an insta\-kill. Defensive The Cardinal is accompanied at all times by her Orb. This small device orbits her and projects an energy force field that protects her from all attacks. The Cardinal may only be harmed once her orb is destroyed, but she will quickly generate a new orb after a few seconds.

- The Cardinal is, in essence, just an Ascendant colored red but with a lot more hitpoints as befitting a gameplay "boss" character. Most tactics for dealing with Ascendants also apply to her. - The Cardinal is able to continuously summon kett forces during the fight. This means all due focus should be on her and not the minions, only thinning out the herd if they become too inconvenient.

- Within the Catholic Church, the word "cardinal" is the title of a senior ecclesiastical priest, immediately below the Pope in rank and appointed by him to assist him as a member of the College of Cardinals. Catholic cardinals also traditionally wear red vestments and attire, and the word "cardinal" has even evolved to mean a specific shade of red. The word is also used to define something of great or fundamental importance.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 5: The Possibility Space
text: The following is a transcription of the fifth chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 5: The Possibility Space
text: Long before she wrote *Atlas Shrugged*, Russian\-American novelist Ayn Rand was a struggling playwright in the 1930s. Her first play produced in Los Angeles and then on Broadway was *The Night of January 16th*. The story was inspired by the life of Ivan Krueger, \[sic] a businessman who controlled the worldwide market for red phosphorous matches and supposedly committed suicide after facing bankruptcy. In the play, a fictional businessman named Bjorn falls to his death in New York City. Although he left a suicide note, the police suspect his mistress and secretary Karen might have pushed him off the edge for unknown reasons. The purpose of the play is a trial to decide if his death was a suicide or murder. But instead of writing one ending, Rand came up with a brilliant concept. What if she wrote two endings to the trial and, in one of the first bits of interactive narrative on record, let the audience serve as the jury? Every night Broadway theatergoers voted on Karen's guilt or innocence, and the results impacted the final scenes of the play. These days interactive narrative may not be employed frequently on Broadway, but it's often used in the game industry. In Knights of the Old Republic, for instance, Hudson and his team players a natural choice of joining the light or the dark side of the force, which impacts the ending of the game. For Mass Effect, Hudson envisioned a burn\-your\-mouth\-on\-the\-soup level of ambition for the branching narrative. Instead of putting a fork in the road near the end of the game, what if the player could make real choices from the start that would cascade throughout not just the game, but the entire trilogy? For example, a player could choose to kill off a squad mate in the first game and he or she would disappear from the next two games. Or a player's character could fall in love in one game and then, in the sequel, the love interest would remember their relationship. All these choices would compound each other to create a dizzying array of possible outcomes, all of which had to somehow dovetail with an overarching plot. "We had to get comfortable with the idea that a large percentage of our work might be seen by only a very small percentage of players," explains lead cinematics designer Parrish Ley, known to fans for a Facebook page devoted to his extravagant moustache during Mass Effect 2. The vastness of possibility was staggering. It was also scary because, at the same time, Hudson wanted to significantly increase the cinematic production values. It's one thing to change a game's story when you're just dealing with text on the screen or characters with one gesture of animation per line. But for Mass Effect the team envisioned digital actors that had wrinkles in their skin, motion\-captured movements, moving eyes and dramatic voice\-over performances. Like most role\-playing games, choice would extend to in\-game conversations in which players could steer a dialogue exchange in a variety of ways. These conversations in RPGs are supposed to be dramatic, but in most games the tension is fractured: The game pauses every time the player needs to read all the responses and, once the player picks one, the character never reads the line aloud. The Mass Effect team wanted to change this dynamic by giving the player a voice in conversations, which would build more personality and heighten the drama. The conversation mechanic would further be enhanced by a dialogue wheel that would let players rapidly select the tenor of a response — neutral, friendly, hostile, investigative — then have the character act it out inside the game world. Just like the jury in Ayn Rand's play decides between guilty and innocent, the player would render his or her verdict in each scene by picking an option on the dialogue wheel. On top of all this the game would track the player's morality by logging whether the choices were heroic (paragon) or ruthless (renegade), eventually leading to different story paths. All these variables would be layered on top of the usual BioWare choices: You could play as either a male or female character, and select from various alien and human characters to accompany you on missions as teammates. When it was all added up, the possible permutations and combinations were mind\-numbing. Preston Watamaniuk and his design team realized they were going to have to keep track of 700 different "plot states," a dizzying array of 1s and 0s that could impact something as small as the tone in a line of dialogue or as big as eliminating an entire character from key scenes. The idea was brilliant but terrifying, especially as these choices had to be carried over from one game to the next.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 5: The Possibility Space
text: When it was all added up, the possible permutations and combinations were mind\-numbing. Preston Watamaniuk and his design team realized they were going to have to keep track of 700 different "plot states," a dizzying array of 1s and 0s that could impact something as small as the tone in a line of dialogue or as big as eliminating an entire character from key scenes. The idea was brilliant but terrifying, especially as these choices had to be carried over from one game to the next. "The checks we were writing on Mass Effect 1 — we had no idea how we were going to pay \[them] off down the road," admits Ley. Ask anyone on the Mass Effect team about the way Casey Hudson directs a game and you hear one word in response: vision. Hudson is a true polymath who knows how to draw, how to program, how to design in 3D, even how to compose music. (He also dabbles in architecture and designed the house he lives in with his wife and two sons.) All these talents allow him to speak the language of the artists and programmers and to get his hands dirty when he wants something realized a certain way. That's exactly what happened one night in 2007\. After work Hudson headed to the local supermarket, bought some slabs of meat, and spent most of the night photographing a combination of steaks, circuit boards, ribs and screws in his basement. The next day he showed up at work with the photos, which formed the backbone of a mysterious dream\-like sequence the main character, Commander Shepard, sees in Mass Effect after being exposed to an alien beacon on the planet Eden Prime. The fact that Hudson was able to finally focus on story points underscored the progress the team was making. By early 2007 the plot was stabilizing and writers such as Mac Walters — a BioWare fan who got the job after building a user\-made add\-on to Neverwinter Nights on his Pentium laptop — started to work on defining the personalities of the various aliens. Shauna Perry, who ran a troupe of corporate improv comedians and managed a folk band on the side, began auditioning actors who might able to bring the characters to life. First choices didn't always work out as planned. A character named Ashley, the male Commander's love interest, was originally voiced by E.G. Daily from *The Powerpuff Girls*, only to be re\-cast after none of the team members felt they could fall in love with the character. Love would play a role in Mass Effect, but the main plotline would involve Commander Shepard's "call to glory," as Hudson put it. Sent to investigate a mysterious beacon left behind by an extinct alien race, now known as the Protheans, Shepard would cross paths with Saren, a Turian \[sic] alien who double\-crosses The Alliance, a United Nations\-like body in charge of the galaxy. \[sic] Saren works on building his own army of machines, led by sentient AI robots named the Geth \[sic] that had revolted against their creators, the nomadic Quarians. \[sic] Later in the game players would realize that Saren had been brainwashed by the Reapers to do their bidding (a link back to the "master slaves" idea), the first ominous sign of the Reapers' pending return. As development progressed, the team had to adjust certain elements of the story. The Geth, for example, just weren't scary enough. They were supposed to be cold\-blooded killing machines, but in one early scene a Geth ran over to help his robot friend was shot on the battlefield. Sitting on the "couch of truth" in the office, a place where the team leads reviewed the game's progress, Watts saw the sequence and began singing "Lean on Me." To make the Geth scarier an idea was hatched: What if they impaled dead humans on 20\-foot\-high mechanical spikes that pump the cadavers full of cybernetics and turn them into mindless killing husks? Yep, much better. By the spring of 2007 it was clear that parts of Mass Effect's original vision, hugely ambitious from the start, would never be realized. The entire online Xbox Live trading system was scotched, and Walters' idea of a plot about a shadowy organization named Cerberus, which conducted human experiments on a planet named Misery, was designed but never made it into the game. Similarly, a volcanic mining planet named Caleston was planned as a level but cut due to production delays. (Some of those story elements folded into the player's adventures on the planet Therum.) More than anything else the game's combat system continued to be refined as the team balanced the desire for a mainstream action\-oriented experience with the company's roots in a deep role\-playing game with skills, stats and progression.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 5: The Possibility Space
text: The entire online Xbox Live trading system was scotched, and Walters' idea of a plot about a shadowy organization named Cerberus, which conducted human experiments on a planet named Misery, was designed but never made it into the game. Similarly, a volcanic mining planet named Caleston was planned as a level but cut due to production delays. (Some of those story elements folded into the player's adventures on the planet Therum.) More than anything else the game's combat system continued to be refined as the team balanced the desire for a mainstream action\-oriented experience with the company's roots in a deep role\-playing game with skills, stats and progression. By the summer of 2007 one pivotal moment in the game was starting to feel exactly like Hudson's vision for a cinematic adventure with interactive choice and consequence. On Virmire, a humid, tropical planet seen near the end of the game, the team designed a showdown between the player and Wrex, a Krogan \[sic] mercenary that is a key part of the story. This race of dinosaur\-like creatures was facing extinction due to the genophage, a plague created by another alien species, the Salarians, \[sic] which wiped out the ability for Krogans \[sic] to procreate. Saren found a cure to the genophage and was planning to breed a Krogan army to join the Geth, but Shepard is given orders to destroy the base, the cure and, of course, Saren. Wrex, on the other hand, has different priorities. He'd rather save the cure and the future of his civilization. Does Wrex see your side of the story or do you have to kill this character you've come to love? The outcome of the scene is entirely up to the player's dialogue choices. Other elements come into play, too. If the player had helped Wrex earlier in the game by retrieving his family armor, he trusts you and it is easier to convince him of the bigger picture. Most games have showdown sequences like this but they are a Hobson's choice — you know there is really just one way to advance the plot. (Hint: You shoot the guy and move on.) But in Mass Effect the story can go either way. The real fun comes when players talk with their friends and they discover that yes, they could have made the other choice for a different outcome. By September the team was about to make another discovery: Mass Effect was inches away from being finished. On September 25, 2007, at 5:05 p.m., Casey Hudson emailed the team with the news. "Congratulations team! Last night's build, 635, has been submitted to Microsoft as RC2 — the first build with a real possibility of being 'the one,'" he wrote. The Mass Effect trilogy was about to officially begin.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 9: The Illusive Date
text: The following is a transcription of the ninth chapter of Geoff Keighley's documentary work The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3, published in 2012\.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 9: The Illusive Date
text: "Only one thing is certain: If Shepard doesn't bring help soon, there won't be an Earth left to save." With that line of dialogue from an unnamed soldier pinned down in London during an all\-out Reaper invasion, Mass Effect 3 was officially announced in December 2010 at the Spike Video Game Awards for a holiday 2011 release. Fans were thrilled that the final chapter of the trilogy was less than a year from release, but back in Edmonton the team was starting to worry about its aggressive deadline relative to the scope of the project. By March those worries turned into real concern. Aaron Flynn, BioWare's general manager, had risen through the programming ranks at the company after giving up a career as a fruit fly geneticist. As he grappled with Dragon Age II, a BioWare product that was not turning out quite as the studio had hoped, in March 2011 he also faced a roomful of Mass Effect developers who expressed concern about hitting the promised holiday release date. Walking back to his office, he called Muzyka and left a message saying that they should talk right away. Within 24 hours Flynn was on the line with Frank Gibeau, the president of Electronic Arts' games label, explaining that things were not coming together as quickly as the team had hoped. The decision was made to move the game's launch out of a crowded holiday season and into March of 2012\. The team had bought a few more months of development, but Watamaniuk and Hudson knew that even with extra time they needed to make a few trims to the story. "It's not how much work you've done, it's how much work you have left to do," Watamaniuk told the team in a meeting at which the scope of the game was discussed. After much deliberation, what was known as the first "CAT" or catalyst mission, where the player would meet a Prothean alien for the first time, was removed from the overarching plot. The mission would later be completed as post\-release content, but to many on the team it was a heartbreaking loss. Of course no decision on a game like Mass Effect is made in isolation. The removal of the Prothean mission had a domino effect on other elements of the story. In the original plot a key mission would take place on the planet Thessia, the Asari \[sic] home world. Part of that mission was to involve the Illusive Man kidnapping the Prothean and extracting information from him. But due to the character's removal from the main story, the designers needed to change around the Thessia mission so the Illusive Man picks up the Prothean data in another way. Other changes were made as well. Originally, the game's second CAT mission was planned as the downfall of Thessia, to be followed by CAT 3, a Citadel\-based mission in which Shepard finds out that Cerberus is taking over the space station. Now the team was questioning that order. Cerberus was showing up too late in the plot, and there needed to be a mission later in the story that would remind players of the grim state of the galaxy. The decision was made to switch the order of these two key missions. Once again this had story implications, as any character who died during the Citadel mission would now be unavailable to appear on Thessia. As the seasons began to change in Edmonton and spring arrived, the gameplay team worked to further tighten the combat with the addition of grenades that forced players to keep moving and not stay too long in one cover position. The multiplayer mode was an immense help for the single player campaign as well, as more designers were working around the clock to refine the core action mechanics. Speaking of high\-stakes action, for months the team couldn't quite figure out how they wanted to deal with the threat of the Illusive Man and his inevitable showdown with Shepard. A Cerberus assassin named Kai Leng — with a snake tattoo on his back — would be introduced as Shepard's foil throughout much of the story, but ultimately everyone knew there needed to be a resolution to the philosophical battle between the Illusive Man, who wants to control the Reapers to protect humanity, and Shepard, who wants them outright destroyed. For a few months there were plans on the table for the Illusive Man to be further indoctrinated by the Reapers near the end of the game and turn into a larger, more cybernetic monster the player would have to battle. Although art was created for this sequence, it was ultimately dropped because it felt too predictable to end the series on a massive boss battle.

page: The Final Hours of Mass Effect 3/Chapter 9: The Illusive Date
text: For a few months there were plans on the table for the Illusive Man to be further indoctrinated by the Reapers near the end of the game and turn into a larger, more cybernetic monster the player would have to battle. Although art was created for this sequence, it was ultimately dropped because it felt too predictable to end the series on a massive boss battle. While work continued in Edmonton, in early June Hudson and Corey Gaspur jumped on a plane and headed to Los Angeles for the annual E3 video game expo. Appearing on stage at Electronic Arts' annual press conference, Hudson announced that Mass Effect 3 would arrive on March 6, 2012, and demonstrated a sequence with Shepard battling a monstrous Reaper on the Quarian \[sic] home world of Rannoch. For the next three days the team demonstrated the game to the press, retailers and special guests, at times sneaking up to 30 people in a demo room designed for 11\. Returning from Los Angeles, the team took a few weeks to slow down before the final push began in earnest. Enjoying the warm Edmonton summer, Hudson went out one night for a jog and listened to John Carpenter's *Escape from New York* soundtrack on his iPod. Another night he just stayed at home and tried to learn how to play his favorite new song, *Death Cab for Cutie*'s "You Are a Tourist." As he thought about the game he realized that there was still much to do, and started to accept that some player requests, like a mission set on the Turian \[sic] home world of Palaven, just weren't going to be possible this time around. The next six months were going to be a brutal and unforgiving race to the finish line. So before he was lost to the world of triage meetings, bug reports and 15\-hour days, Hudson wanted to clear his mind by taking his wife out for a romantic flight over the mountains of Jasper. "Went for a little flight above the Rockies with my sweetie," he Tweeted from his iPhone on Canada Day, July 1\. Flying through the clouds, Hudson felt completely in control of the world around him. As he landed back at the airport he pulled his plane into the hanger, locked it up and knew he probably wouldn't be back as soon as he wished. The hardest days on Mass Effect 3 were still to come — although Hudson had no idea just how bad things were about to get.

section: Video: Casey Explains Why They Abandoned the Illusive Man Sequence
text: **Casey Hudson**: Well, resolving the storyline is one thing... And then, the other side of what we need to resolve in a video game, is resolving the gameplay. And... you know, you're progressing, you're building up your powers and getting stronger as a character. And then, what do you do with that in the end? And usually, you fight some sort of boss. And sometimes, it's a giant tentacle creature, regardless of what your story is really about. And, you know... So, obviously, some of the original ideas for where you would end up at the end of the story involved some kind of giant tentacle creature that would come out of nowhere and be the boss for Mass Effect 3. But, you know, it was just so video\-gamey, and nothing that we did to, you know, kind of work it into the themes, really answered the fact that ultimately it just felt like there was an end boss for the sake of having an end boss. And that raises the question of, you know, like, if video games are a medium for storytelling, do they always have to have an end boss?

section: Video: Casey on Stage for the E3 2011 Demo of Mass Effect 3
text: **Casey Hudson**: Hey, everyone. I'm Casey Hudson. Now, the Mass Effect series was designed from the very beginning to be a trilogy. The first two games have been foreshadowing an all\-out galactic war with an ancient machine race known as the Reapers. Well, on March 6, 2012, that war will begin. The Earth has been taken, and the Reapers have laid a path of destruction in their wake. As Commander Shepard, only you can rally the forces of the galaxy to mount a counter\-offensive big enough to stop them. Now, we're giving our longtime fans the amazing opportunity that they've been waiting for to see how all the choices that they've made along the way have led to this critical breaking point. And we're giving players new to the series an opportunity to jump into the Mass Effect universe when the action and the tension will be at its absolute peak. This is all out galactic war. So let's jump into a live demo played by our combat designer, Corey Gaspur. In this demo, Shepard is attempting to destroy a Reaper base. And with the Normandy overhead and a fleet in orbit, Commander Shepard's going to call in some heavy firepower. *(Gameplay from Priority: Rannoch)* **Casey Hudson**: All right. Now that's just a small taste of what we're doing with the scale of the battles in Mass Effect 3\. But Mass Effect 3 isn't just about these huge moments. It's intense action combat, it's decisions with huge consequences and sacrifice, and it's all wrapped up in a story of tremendous emotional impact. This is why Mass Effect 3 will be the best game in the series. Find out for yourselves on March 6, 2012, when the Reapers arrive. So, thank you. Make sure you visit Origin.com to see even more from Mass Effect 3\. And right now, the world debut of our first gameplay trailer, the fall of Earth.

section: Who's Who: The Mass Effect 3 Squad
text: - Ashley Williams: Recently promoted to Spectre status, Lieutenant Commander Ashley Williams is a career military officer with the Systems Alliance Marines and a potential love interest for the Commander. Born to a military family, Williams enlisted directly out of high school, splitting time between Earth and hostile environment training on Saturn's moon, Titan. - EDI: Voiced by actress Tricia Helfer, EDI (Enhanced Defense Intelligence) is the Normandy's on\-board artificial intelligence known for her "equitable working relationship" with Joker, the ship's captain. \[sic] In Mass Effect 3 she takes on a physical form by gaining control of a Cerberus infiltration unit's body. - Garrus Vakarian: A turian who began military training at age 15, Garrus is a C\-Sec security officer who headed up the investigation of Saren's rogue activities in the first Mass Effect. Posing as the tactical genius Archangel on Omega in Mass Effect 2, Garrus reunites with the player both in that game and for Mass Effect 3\. - James Vega: New for Mass Effect 3, James is one of the best soldiers in the Alliance. He's young, brash and dangerous. Some see Commander Shepard's newest recruit as reckless, but James will defend Earth to his dying breath. He is voiced by actor Freddie Prinze Jr and was inspired by the soldiers in the book WAR by Sebastian Junger. - Kaidan Alenko: Kaidan commands 1st Special Operations Biotic Company, a specialized arm of covert operations within the Alliance Army. At the Alliance Special Warfare Center and School, he takes the best and the brightest from the Ascension Project at Grissom Academy and trains them to be elite biotic soldiers. - Liara T'Soni: Dr. Liara T'Soni is an Asari \[sic] information broker with a background in scientific research on Prothean technology. Born on Thessia in 2077, she is the only child of the late Matriarch Benezia, although mother and daughter became estranged in the years before Benezia was indoctrinated by the Reaper known as Sovereign. - Tali'Zorah nar Rayya: A fan favorite, Tali is a Quarian \[sic] whose masked face has never been seen by players. Born aboard a spaceship, she—like all Quarians—must wear an envirosuit due to her weak immune system. In Mass Effect, Tali discovers that Saren is responsible for the attacks on Eden Prime and shares this information with the player.
