They spread so fast that the Hierarchy's influence over the new colonies wore thin. Local colonial chieftains, known as Primarchs, began seeking autonomy. Without the central government's galvanizing influence, colonies grew isolated and xenophobic. Colonists took to wearing emblems or facial markings to distinguish themselves from other colonies, and open hostility became common. Around 300 BCE this erupted into open war — the beginning of the Unification Wars. The Hierarchy officially stayed neutral at first, keeping to a strict policy of diplomacy and refusing to intervene militarily. The conflicts were sparked by nationalistic pride but were almost always fought over disputed territory. Years passed with little progress; collateral damage rose sharply as the number of factions fell. With no end in sight and no real demands beyond "give me all your territory," the Hierarchy finally had to intervene to stop the continuing loss of Turian life. After years of fighting, the Primarch chieftains were too weak to resist and had likely lost the support of their own people. When terms were offered, they were forced to end the conflicts and renew their allegiance to the Hierarchy. Peace was restored, though it took several decades for the animosity between colonists to fade.

page: The Turian Hierarchy Before the Citadel — Early History
text: To this day most Turians still wear the facial markings of their home colony. Lacking markings is looked down on: the Turian term "bare-faced" means someone beguiling or not to be trusted, and is also slang for a politician.

page: The Turian Hierarchy Before the Citadel — Early History
section: A war machine without a war
text: Reunited under the Hierarchy, Palaven and its colonies returned to being a prosperous nation with the military at its center. Despite having no enemies to fight, the Turian navy expanded to enormous size, culminating in at least 32 individual fleets. The Turian war machine needed no war to keep turning.

page: The Turian Hierarchy Before the Citadel — Early History
text: About a thousand years later, around 704 CE, the Hierarchy made first contact with an alien civilization: a conglomerate of species led by the Asari and Salarians known as the Citadel Council. The Council welcomed the Turians and offered immediate membership in Citadel space — an offer that, as the Turians would learn, came with an ulterior motive. <!-- transcript unclear: the video ends here; the "ulterior motive" is a lead-in to the Krogan Rebellions / the Turians being recruited to fight the krogan, not stated outright in this source. -->

page: Two Races We Never See — the Reloi and the "Virtual Aliens"
text: **Summary:** Two minor Mass Effect species that never appear in-game, known only from Cerberus Daily News items around 2185–2186: the Reloi, an avian race from the planet Tervest who briefly joined the galactic community and then withdrew rather than face the Reapers; and an unnamed race of "virtual aliens" who fled a supernova ~8,000 years ago as roughly a billion uploaded consciousnesses aboard a computer-run starship, and who negotiated asylum by inhabiting the bodies of volunteers.

page: Two Races We Never See — the Reloi and the "Virtual Aliens"
text: The Reloi are an avian, spacefaring race, known to the elcor long before they were known to the wider galaxy. According to Cerberus Daily News (a Mass Effect 2 feed), they were discovered by the asari in 2184 and welcomed to the galactic community in 2185: council-sponsored shuttles arrived at Tervest, the Reloi homeworld, bearing visitors and gifts of goodwill. After the welcoming ceremonies a Reloi delegation was sent to the Citadel to learn galactic law, culture, history, alien biology, and mass effect technology. The contact ceremonies caused an outbreak of an alien flu among the Reloi, which prompted them to wear environmental suits in the presence of other species. In 2186 the Reloi delegation withdrew completely from the Citadel and isolated themselves on Tervest, both unwilling and unable to fight the Reapers. A species representative named Arrika stated: "We have no wish to battle those who have yet to wrong us, nor have we the capability." The Reloi also planned to destroy their orbital satellites and observation equipment, hoping the Reapers would take them for a pre-spaceflight civilization and pass them over. Whether this worked is unknown — the rest of the galaxy was preoccupied with the war. There are no official depictions of the Reloi. All that is established is that they are avian in appearance, possess feathers, and would likely have been seen in environmental suits around other species because of the flu outbreak.

page: Two Races We Never See — the Reloi and the "Virtual Aliens"
text: This race has no known name; they are referred to only as the virtual aliens. About 8,000 years before the trilogy, their homeworld's star was about to go supernova. To survive, they built a starship equipped with a network of supercomputers and transferred the consciousnesses of roughly one billion of their people into it, along with an entire virtual world for them to inhabit. An AI was left to pilot the ship and maintain the simulation. The ship then drifted through space for millennia. In 2185 the starship entered a salarian-inhabited system, seeking help because the energy source keeping the ship and the virtual world running was failing. When the salarians found the "ghost ship" they initially feared it was the vanguard of a Reaper attack because of the onboard AI. Contact with the AI was first made by a human exobiologist, Dr. Jordan Deitweiler, who learned of the virtual world, its population, and the energy problem. The Citadel Council was wary of the AI and reluctant to help. Deitweiler entered the virtual world to warn its inhabitants and returned with an offer: the virtual aliens would trade their advanced technology and knowledge in exchange for assistance. The Council classified all matters involving the ship as top secret, but is understood to have assisted in the end. About a month later it emerged that a representative for the virtual aliens, Ambassador Sygan, had been using Dr. Deitweiler's body to visit the Citadel and speak with the Council — revealing that the virtual aliens could re-enter the real world in the bodies of people who entered their world. Sygan sought asylum, saying she was one of many who wished to leave the virtual world. A volunteer took Deitweiler's place so he could return to his own body while his was used by Sygan. After this was announced, around 400 individuals of various races also stepped forward to swap places with virtual aliens. The implication is that in Mass Effect 2 and 3 the player may have encountered some of these virtual aliens — now living in the bodies of the volunteers — without knowing it. Those who left the virtual world would, a year later, be caught in the Reaper war.
